# Meterless Engines in the Angular To-Do App

This app implements all four Meterless engines as browser-safe TypeScript ports. The engines are not installed as npm packages; their logic lives in `src/app/engines/` and is wired into the app through services.

The original design review is superseded: the engines are now part of the product, while ordinary CRUD still bypasses them.

## What is implemented

| Engine           | Port location                 | App role                                                                 | Persistence key                |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| **Scout Intent** | `src/app/engines/scout/`      | Classify natural-language input, block injections, gate risky actions    | None; execution contracts only |
| **H-MEM**        | `src/app/engines/hmem/`       | Remember and retrieve user preferences and notes                         | `angular-todo-app.hmem.v1`     |
| **World Model**  | `src/app/engines/world-model/`| Event-sourced task entities, audit trail, merge proposals                | `angular-todo-app.world.v1`    |
| **Markovian**    | `src/app/engines/markovian/`  | Generate bounded plans with per-run chunk configuration and efficiency   | `angular-todo-app.markovian.v1`|

Task records remain in `TaskStore` under `angular-todo-app.tasks`. The engines observe or assist; they do not replace the task store as the commit point.

## Runtime flow

```text
user input
  -> Scout Intent        classify, guard, route
  -> H-MEM               remember or recall preferences
  -> World Model         ground task entities
  -> Markovian           plan long-horizon goals
  -> TaskStore           commit accepted task changes
  -> World Model         append task events
```

Normal UI actions (add, toggle, edit, delete, filter) still go directly from the component to `TaskStore`. The assistant is an additional path, not a wrapper around every click.

## Scout Intent

`ScoutService` loads the app registry from `src/app/engines/scout/app-registry.ts` with the `default` and `adversarial-tight` policy packs.

- Intents cover task add/complete/uncomplete/delete/rename/list/filter/summary/plan, memory remember/recall/forget, and a safe `GENERAL` fallback.
- High-risk actions such as deleting all tasks require explicit confirmation in the assistant panel.
- Prompt-injection patterns are blocked before any action runs.
- Every decision produces a signed execution contract; the app verifies it through `ScoutService.verify`.

The eval adapter is `eval/scout-entry.ts`. It loads the spec fixture registry from `SCOUT_INTENTS_PATH` when provided, otherwise it uses the app registry.

## H-MEM

`MemoryService` wraps a browser-safe `HMEM` instance.

- Explicit "remember" requests are stored as long-term memory with source `user`.
- Recall uses hybrid ranking; if a generic recall query has no strong match, the panel falls back to recent memories.
- Feedback, conflicts, sleep, and dreaming are available in the engine API, but the current UI surfaces memory creation, retrieval, and deletion only.
- Persistence is injected through a localStorage adapter; the engine core has no filesystem dependency.

## World Model

`WorldModelService` owns a `WorldModel` with namespace `todo`.

- Each task is an entity keyed by the stable external key `todo:<task-id>`.
- `TaskStore` syncs add, toggle, and rename operations with `upsertEntitySync`.
- Delete operations append a tombstone and archive the entity.
- The activity panel reads recent events and audit entries; merge proposals are available in the engine API for future review UI.
- Persistence is injected; the browser port does not write `.world/` files.

## Markovian

`PlanningService` wraps a `Markovian` instance with a local deterministic generator.

- "Plan ..." requests run one bounded chunk, so the plan completes without an external model.
- Every run records its own `chunkConfig` snapshot, as required by the spec.
- The assistant shows the plan and the run's efficiency percentage.
- History and cumulative stats persist across reloads.
- The generator can be replaced with a provider-backed `generator` or `stepFn` without changing the engine.

## Browser adaptations

The reference implementations are Node-oriented. The ports differ in three deliberate ways:

1. **No filesystem access.** `node:fs` and `node:path` imports are removed. H-MEM, World Model, and Markovian history accept injected `load`/`save` persistence adapters. The app supplies localStorage adapters.
2. **Browser-safe crypto.** Scout uses the dependency-free SHA-256/HMAC implementation in `src/app/engines/shared/crypto.ts` instead of Node crypto.
3. **Synchronous write seams for the UI.** World Model exposes `upsertEntitySync` and `tombstoneSync` so `TaskStore` can project a local mutation immediately. The queued async methods remain available for ingest-style callers.

Internal engine imports are extensionless so the Angular compiler can bundle them. The Node-only Scout adapter imports the engine with an explicit `.ts` extension because it runs under `tsx`.

## Deliberate limits

- The assistant is deterministic and local. There is no remote model, API key, or network dependency.
- Scout's registry covers the app's actual action surface. Adding a new tool means adding an intent, capabilities, examples, and a fixture.
- H-MEM dreaming, sleep consolidation, and conflict auto-resolution are implemented but not exposed in the UI.
- World Model merge proposals are recorded; there is no operator review screen yet.
- Markovian plans are generated locally; long-horizon model-backed planning would replace the generator, not the engine.
- `localStorage` is the only persistence tier. IndexedDB or a backend can replace the adapters without changing engine cores.

## Design rules kept

- `TaskStore` remains the only task mutation point.
- Stable IDs and persisted-record validation are preserved.
- Derived state stays in `computed` signals.
- Components remain presentational and `OnPush`.
- Engines stay framework-free; Angular integration lives in services and components.

# Meterless Engines in the Angular To-Do App

This app implements all four Meterless engines as browser-safe TypeScript ports. The engines are not installed as npm packages; their logic lives in `src/app/engines/` and is wired into the app through services.

The original design review is superseded: the engines are now part of the product, while ordinary CRUD still bypasses them.

## What is implemented

| Engine           | Port location                  | App role                                                               | Persistence key                 |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| **Scout Intent** | `src/app/engines/scout/`       | Classify natural-language input, block injections, gate risky actions  | None; execution contracts only  |
| **H-MEM**        | `src/app/engines/hmem/`        | Remember and retrieve user preferences and notes                       | `angular-todo-app.hmem.v1`      |
| **World Model**  | `src/app/engines/world-model/` | Event-sourced task entities, audit trail, merge proposals              | `angular-todo-app.world.v1`     |
| **Markovian**    | `src/app/engines/markovian/`   | Generate bounded plans with per-run chunk configuration and efficiency | `angular-todo-app.markovian.v1` |

Task records remain in `TaskStore` under `angular-todo-app.tasks`. The engines observe or assist; they do not replace the task store as the commit point.

## Runtime flow

```text
user input
  -> Scout Intent        classify, guard, route
  -> H-MEM               remember or recall preferences
  -> World Model         ground task entities
  -> Markovian           plan long-horizon goals
  -> TaskStore           commit accepted task changes
  -> World Model         append task events
```

Normal UI actions (add, toggle, edit, delete, filter) still go directly from the component to `TaskStore`. The assistant is an additional path, not a wrapper around every click.

## Scout Intent

`ScoutService` loads the app registry from `src/app/engines/scout/app-registry.ts` with the `default` and `adversarial-tight` policy packs.

- Intents cover task add/complete/uncomplete/delete/rename/list/filter/summary/plan, memory remember/recall/forget, and a safe `GENERAL` fallback.
- High-risk actions such as deleting all tasks require explicit confirmation in the assistant panel.
- Prompt-injection patterns are blocked before any action runs.
- Every decision produces a signed execution contract; the app verifies it through `ScoutService.verify`.

The eval adapter is `eval/scout-entry.ts`. It reads the registry path supplied by the harness and passes the parsed registry into the browser core.

## H-MEM

`MemoryService` wraps a browser-safe `HMEM` instance.

- Explicit "remember" requests are stored as long-term memory with source `user`.
- Recall uses hybrid ranking; if a generic recall query has no strong match, the panel falls back to recent memories.
- Feedback, conflicts, sleep, and dreaming are available in the engine API, but the current UI surfaces memory creation, retrieval, and deletion only.
- Persistence is injected through a localStorage adapter; the engine core has no filesystem dependency.

## World Model

`WorldModelService` owns a `WorldModel` with namespace `todo`.

- Each task is an entity keyed by the stable external key `todo:<task-id>`.
- `TaskStore` syncs add, toggle, and rename operations with `upsertEntitySync`.
- Delete operations append a tombstone and archive the entity.
- The activity panel reads recent events and audit entries; merge proposals are available in the engine API for future review UI.
- Persistence is injected; the browser port does not write `.world/` files.

## Markovian

`PlanningService` wraps a `Markovian` instance with a local deterministic generator.

- "Plan ..." requests run one bounded chunk, so the plan completes without an external model.
- Every run records its own `chunkConfig` snapshot, as required by the spec.
- The assistant shows the plan and the run's efficiency percentage.
- History and cumulative stats persist across reloads.
- The generator can be replaced with a provider-backed `generator` or `stepFn` without changing the engine.

## Conformance and eval

Run the suites from a checkout of the Meterless spec. The exact repository path is environment-specific; the commands below use `<meterless-spec>` as the placeholder.

### Scout eval

```bash
cd <meterless-spec>/engines/scout-intent
npm install
SCOUT_IMPL=<angular-todo-app>/eval/scout-entry.ts \
  npx tsx evals/runner/index.ts all
```

## Browser adaptations

The reference implementations are Node-oriented. The ports differ in three deliberate ways:

1. **No filesystem access.** `node:fs` and `node:path` imports are removed. H-MEM, World Model, and Markovian history accept injected `load`/`save` persistence adapters. The app supplies localStorage adapters.
2. **Browser-safe crypto.** Scout uses the dependency-free SHA-256/HMAC implementation in `src/app/engines/shared/crypto.ts` instead of Node crypto.
3. **Synchronous write seams for the UI.** World Model exposes `upsertEntitySync` and `tombstoneSync` so `TaskStore` can project a local mutation immediately. The queued async methods remain available for ingest-style callers.

Internal engine imports are extensionless so the Angular compiler can bundle them. The Node-only Scout adapter imports the engine with an explicit `.ts` extension because it runs under `tsx`.

## Deliberate limits

- The assistant is deterministic and local. There is no remote model, API key, or network dependency.
- Scout's registry covers the app's actual action surface. Adding a new tool means adding an intent, capabilities, examples, and a fixture.
- H-MEM dreaming, sleep consolidation, and conflict auto-resolution are implemented but not exposed in the UI.
- World Model merge proposals are recorded; there is no operator review screen yet.
- Markovian plans are generated locally; long-horizon model-backed planning would replace the generator, not the engine.
- `localStorage` is the only persistence tier. IndexedDB or a backend can replace the adapters without changing engine cores.

## Design rules kept

- `TaskStore` remains the only task mutation point.
- Stable IDs and persisted-record validation are preserved.
- Derived state stays in `computed` signals.
- Components remain presentational and `OnPush`.
- Engines stay framework-free; Angular integration lives in services and components.

# Angular To-Do App

A small, responsive to-do list built with Angular 22, standalone components, signals, and `localStorage`. No backend, no auth, no extra UI libraries.

The app also ships browser-safe ports of the four Meterless engines: **Scout Intent**, **H-MEM**, **World Model**, and **Markovian**.

## Features

- Add, edit, complete, and delete tasks
- Filter by All, Active, and Completed with live counts
- Remaining-task counter
- Tasks persist across refreshes via `localStorage`
- Empty state for each filter
- Keyboard-friendly editing (`Enter` saves, `Escape` cancels, double-click a title to edit)
- Mobile-responsive layout with a minimal, modern UI
- Natural-language assistant: add, complete, rename, delete, filter, and summarize tasks
- Scout Intent routing with prompt-injection blocking and confirmation for destructive actions
- H-MEM preference memory with retrieval, persistence, and a trust ledger
- World Model event log with task entities and an activity panel
- Markovian plan generation with per-run chunk configuration and efficiency stats

## Run it

```bash
npm install
npm start
```

Open `http://localhost:4200`.

## Verify it

```bash
npm test        # Vitest unit tests
npm run build   # production build
```

Engine conformance and Scout eval commands are documented in [docs/meterless-fit.md](docs/meterless-fit.md).

## Structure

```text
src/app/
  models/task.model.ts                  Task and filter types
  services/task-store.ts                Signal store, derived views, localStorage
  services/scout.service.ts             Scout Intent facade
  services/memory.service.ts            H-MEM facade and persistence
  services/world-model.service.ts       World Model facade and task sync
  services/planning.service.ts          Markovian facade and persistence
  services/assistant.service.ts         Natural-language action executor
  services/persistence.ts               Shared localStorage JSON helpers
  engines/scout/                        Browser-safe Scout port
  engines/hmem/                         Browser-safe H-MEM port
  engines/world-model/                  Browser-safe World Model port
  engines/markovian/                    Browser-safe Markovian port
  engines/shared/crypto.ts              SHA-256, HMAC, canonical JSON
  directives/autofocus.ts               Focus helper for inline editing
  components/task-input/                Add-task form
  components/task-filters/              All / Active / Completed control
  components/task-item/                 One task row with edit and delete
  components/assistant-panel/           Chat, confirmations, plan output
  components/memory-panel/              Remembered preferences
  components/world-panel/               Event and audit activity
  app.ts / app.html / app.css           Page shell and empty state
```

`TaskStore` remains the only place that mutates tasks. Components are presentational and emit events; derived values (`visibleTasks`, `remainingCount`, `counts`) are `computed` signals. Ordinary CRUD stays on the direct path: component -> `TaskStore` -> `localStorage`.

The assistant path is:

```text
user input
  -> Scout Intent        classify, guard, route
  -> H-MEM               remember or recall preferences
  -> World Model         ground task entities
  -> Markovian           plan long-horizon goals
  -> TaskStore           commit accepted task changes
  -> World Model         append events
```

## Meterless engines

See [docs/meterless-fit.md](docs/meterless-fit.md) for the implementation map, conformance results, persistence keys, and deliberate limits.

## Documentation conventions

- Folder and file names use lowercase kebab-case, except the industry-standard `README.md`.

# Testing

This folder owns the test strategy, commands, and expected results for the app and its Meterless engine ports.

## Start here

- [Meterless Engines Testing Guide](meterless-engines-testing-guide.md) — full manual and automated test guide for the natural-language assistant, Scout Intent, H-MEM, World Model, and Markovian.
- [Meterless Engines implementation map](../meterless-fit.md) — architecture, persistence keys, and engine limits.

## Fast verification

```bash
npm install
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false
npm run build
```

Expected on the current implementation:

- **37 Vitest tests pass** across 7 spec files.
- **Production build succeeds** with no budget errors.
- **Scout eval** passes all thresholds.
- **H-MEM conformance** passes 13/13 checks.
- **World Model conformance** passes 8/8 checks.
- **Markovian conformance** passes 8/8 checks.

## Test layers

| Layer           | Tool                                      | What it proves                                                       |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Unit            | Angular CLI unit-test builder + Vitest    | Store math, persistence, engine service behavior                     |
| Integration     | Angular `TestBed` + jsdom                 | Assistant intent -> action -> store -> engine side effects           |
| Component       | Angular `TestBed` + jsdom                 | App shell and engine panels render                                   |
| Conformance     | Meterless runners under `tsx`             | Engine invariants that are independent of this app                   |
| Eval            | Scout eval harness under `tsx`            | Intent accuracy, injection recall/precision, tool routing            |
| Production build| Angular AOT build                         | Templates, types, CSS budgets, and bundling                          |

## Test data reset

The app persists to `localStorage`. To reset all app state, open DevTools and run:

```js
localStorage.clear();
location.reload();
```

To reset only one subsystem, remove its key:

```js
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.tasks');
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.hmem.v1');
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.world.v1');
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.markovian.v1');
```

## Related

- [Documentation index](../README.md)
- [Project README](../../README.md)

args.content:
# Meterless Engines Testing Guide

- **Applies to:** `angular-todo-app`
- **Last verified:** 2026-10-23
- **Test runner:** Angular CLI 22 unit-test builder + Vitest 5 + jsdom
- **Engine source:** browser-safe ports under `src/app/engines/`
- **Spec source:** a separate Meterless checkout; commands use `<meterless-spec>` as the placeholder

This guide explains how to verify every user-facing engine feature, what each test proves, how to run the automated suites, how to run the Meterless conformance and eval harnesses, and how to diagnose failures.

---

## 1. Scope

### In scope

- Natural-language assistant actions: add, complete, reopen, rename, delete, filter, list, and summarize tasks.
- Scout Intent routing, clarification, signed execution contracts, prompt-injection blocking, and destructive-action confirmation.
- H-MEM preference memory: remember, recall, forget, persistence, retrieval, and trust-ledger entries.
- World Model event log: task entities, upserts, tombstones, audit entries, and the Activity panel.
- Markovian plan generation: chunk configuration snapshot, marker cleanup, efficiency stats, and history persistence.
- Build, type, template, and CSS-budget verification.

### Out of scope

- Load testing, browser matrix testing, visual regression testing, accessibility certification, and penetration testing.
- Remote model providers. The current assistant is deterministic and local.
- Multi-user concurrency, backend sync, and IndexedDB migration.
- H-MEM dreaming, sleep consolidation, and conflict auto-resolution UI, which exist in the engine API but are not exposed in the app.
- World Model merge-review UI, which records proposals but has no operator screen.

---

## 2. Test layers

| Layer            | Command or entry point                                | What it proves                                                                 | Runtime      |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------ |
| Unit             | `npm test -- --watch=false`                           | Store math, persistence, service behavior, engine-service integration          | jsdom        |
| Focused unit     | `npm test -- --watch=false --include=<spec>`          | One spec file in isolation                                                     | jsdom        |
| Named test       | `npm test -- --watch=false --filter="<regex>"`        | One suite or test name                                                         | jsdom        |
| Component        | Included in the unit suite                            | App shell and engine panels render without template errors                     | jsdom        |
| Production build | `npm run build`                                       | AOT templates, TypeScript, bundling, and CSS budgets                           | Node         |
| Engine conformance | Meterless runner under `tsx`                        | Engine invariants independent of Angular                                       | Node + `tsx` |
| Scout eval       | Meterless eval harness under `tsx`                    | Intent accuracy, injection recall/precision, tool routing, clarification rate  | Node + `tsx` |
| Manual smoke     | `npm start` + browser                                 | Real DOM, real `localStorage`, real clicks and keyboard input                  | Browser      |

---

## 3. Prerequisites

### 3.1 App dependencies

From the app root:

```bash
cd angular-todo-app
npm install
```

Verify the toolchain:

```bash
node --version
npm --version
npx ng version
```

Expected: Angular CLI 22.x, Node compatible with the app, and npm available. In this workspace `mise.toml` pins Node `26.10.0`; if your shell reports `mise ERROR No version is set for shim: npm` or `node`, run commands through the pinned toolchain:

```bash
mise x node@26.10.0 -- npm install
mise x node@26.10.0 -- npm test -- --watch=false
```

### 3.2 Meterless spec checkout

The conformance and eval runners live in a separate checkout:

```text
<meterless-spec>/
  engines/
    scout-intent/
      evals/runner/index.ts
      evals/fixtures/intents.json
      evals/config/thresholds.yaml
      evals/regression-set/v1/
    hmem/conformance/runner.ts
    world-model/conformance/runner.ts
    markovian/conformance/runner.ts
```

The app does not vendor the runners. Point the environment variables at the app implementations.

### 3.3 `tsx` for Node runners

The conformance and eval runners import TypeScript directly. Install `tsx` in the spec checkout or use a checkout that already has it:

```bash
cd <meterless-spec>/engines/scout-intent
npm install
```

If the runner reports `Cannot find module 'tsx'`, run from that folder so `npx` resolves the local binary, or install `tsx` globally.

### 3.4 Clean state

Tests clear `localStorage` in `beforeEach`. Manual testing should also start clean:

```js
localStorage.clear();
location.reload();
```

---

## 4. Ten-minute verification

Use this sequence when you only need a release-confidence smoke check.

1. Install dependencies: `npm install`.
2. Run the full unit suite: `CI=true npm test -- --watch=false`.
3. Run the production build: `npm run build`.
4. Start the app: `npm start`, then open `http://localhost:4200`.
5. In the assistant, run `Add a task: buy milk`.
6. Run `Complete buy milk`.
7. Run `Rename buy milk to get milk`.
8. Run `Delete get milk`, then click **Confirm**.
9. Run `Remember that I prefer short answers`.
10. Run `What do you remember about me?`.
11. Run `Plan my week`.
12. Confirm the Activity panel shows task events and the Memory panel shows one memory.
13. Reload the page and confirm the memory and activity survive.
14. Optionally run the four engine harnesses from section 12.

Expected: all assistant actions produce a success message, the task list and panels update immediately, and no console errors appear.

---

## 5. Command reference

### 5.1 Run every test

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false
```

Expected:

```text
Test Files  7 passed (7)
Tests       37 passed (37)
```

### 5.2 Run one spec file

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/assistant.service.spec.ts
```

Expected: 16 tests pass.

Other useful targets:

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/scout.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/memory.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/world-model.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/planning.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/task-store.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/app.spec.ts
```

### 5.3 Run one named test

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --filter="blocks prompt injection"
```

The `--filter` value is a regular expression matched against suite and test names.

### 5.4 List discovered tests

```bash
npx ng test --list-tests
```

### 5.5 Build

```bash
npm run build
```

Expected: `Application bundle generation complete` and no budget errors. The current initial bundle is about 232 kB raw, well below the 500 kB warning threshold.

### 5.6 Development server

```bash
npm start
```

Open `http://localhost:4200`. The app is client-rendered; the first paint happens after Angular boots.

### 5.7 Watch mode

```bash
npm test
```

Vitest stays open and reruns affected specs on change.

### 5.8 Coverage

Coverage is not configured in this app. The command below fails until a coverage provider is installed:

```bash
npm test -- --watch=false --coverage
```

To enable it, install one of:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @vitest/coverage-v8
# or
npm install --save-dev @vitest/coverage-istanbul
```

Then run:

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --coverage --coverage-reporters=text-summary
```

---

## 6. Feature 1 — Natural-language assistant

### 6.1 What it does

The assistant accepts free text in the right-hand panel and turns it into a task action, a memory action, or a plan. It is local and deterministic; no network call is made.

The relevant files are:

| File                                             | Responsibility                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `src/app/components/assistant-panel/`            | Chat UI, input, pending confirmation buttons                             |
| `src/app/services/assistant.service.ts`          | Submit lifecycle, intent execution, task matching, user-facing messages  |
| `src/app/services/scout.service.ts`              | Intent classification, risk assessment, contract signing                |
| `src/app/services/task-store.ts`                 | The only task mutation point                                             |
| `src/app/services/memory.service.ts`             | H-MEM remember/recall/forget                                             |
| `src/app/services/planning.service.ts`           | Markovian plan generation                                                |
| `src/app/services/world-model.service.ts`        | Task entity sync and event persistence                                   |

### 6.2 Request lifecycle

```text
AssistantPanel input
  -> AssistantService.submit(text)
  -> ScoutService.decide(text)
  -> Decision
       |-- clarification? -> show question, stop
       |-- risk.block?    -> show error, stop
       |-- risk.high?     -> set pending confirmation, stop
       `-- otherwise      -> execute intent
  -> TaskStore / MemoryService / PlanningService
  -> WorldModelService side effects
  -> AssistantMessage appended to the chat
```

State signals in `AssistantService`:

- `messages()` — ordered chat messages.
- `busy()` — true while a decision or action is running.
- `pending()` — the high-risk action waiting for confirmation.
- `lastPlan()` — the most recent Markovian run.

### 6.3 Supported intents

| Intent             | Example utterance                         | Action                                              | Risk     |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| `task.add`         | `Add a task: buy milk`                    | Creates a task                                      | low      |
| `task.add`         | `Remind me to call mom`                   | Creates `call mom`                                  | low      |
| `task.complete`    | `Complete buy milk`                       | Marks the matched task complete                     | low      |
| `task.uncomplete`  | `Reopen buy milk`                         | Marks the matched task active                       | low      |
| `task.rename`      | `Rename buy milk to get milk`             | Renames the matched task                            | medium   |
| `task.delete`      | `Delete buy milk`                         | Deletes one task after confirmation                 | high     |
| `task.delete`      | `Clear completed tasks`                   | Deletes completed tasks after confirmation          | high     |
| `task.delete`      | `Delete all tasks`                        | Deletes every task after confirmation               | high     |
| `task.list`        | `Show my tasks`                           | Prints the list                                     | low      |
| `task.filter`      | `Show active tasks`                       | Sets the visible filter                             | low      |
| `task.summary`     | `Summarize my tasks`                      | Prints total/active/completed counts                | low      |
| `task.plan`        | `Plan my week`                            | Runs Markovian and prints a plan                    | low      |
| `memory.remember`  | `Remember that I prefer short answers`    | Adds a long-term memory                             | low      |
| `memory.recall`    | `What do you remember about me?`          | Retrieves memories                                  | low      |
| `memory.forget`    | `Forget that I prefer short answers`      | Deletes the best match                              | medium   |
| `GENERAL`          | `Hello`                                   | Safe fallback message                               | low      |

Task matching is case-insensitive and accepts an exact title, a task title contained in the request, or a request contained in the task title. If no task matches, the assistant returns a message and does not mutate anything.

## 7. Feature 2 — Scout Intent routing and safety

### 7.1 What it does

Scout classifies the request into a registered intent, extracts parameters, assesses risk, optionally asks a clarifying question, builds a tool plan, and issues a signed execution contract.

The app registry is `src/app/engines/scout/app-registry.ts`. The facade is `src/app/services/scout.service.ts`. Policy packs are `default` and `adversarial-tight`.

### 7.2 Risk and confirmation rules

| Risk level | Behavior                                                              |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `low`      | Execute immediately                                                   |
| `medium`   | Execute immediately; no confirmation in the current assistant         |
| `high`     | Set `pending`, show confirmation, execute only after **Confirm**      |
| `block`    | Show an error; do not execute; do not mutate state                    |

`task.delete` is high risk. Requests containing `all` or `every` are escalated to high risk. The confirmation box exposes **Confirm** and **Cancel**; typing `confirm`, `yes`, `do it`, or `approve` also confirms; typing `cancel`, `no`, or `stop` cancels.

## 8. Feature 3 — H-MEM preference memory

### 8.1 What it does

H-MEM stores durable preferences and facts, retrieves them with a hybrid score, and records every lifecycle action in an append-only trust ledger. The app exposes remember, recall, and forget.

Relevant files:

- `src/app/services/memory.service.ts` — app facade and localStorage persistence.
- `src/app/engines/hmem/` — browser-safe engine port.
- `src/app/components/memory-panel/` — memory list and delete controls.

### 8.2 Data model

A memory record carries content, type, layer, timestamps, confidence, source, provenance, domain, namespace, entities, relationships, and optional supersession fields. A record without a source is rejected by construction.

The persistence envelope is:

```json
{
  "store": {
    "records": [],
    "seq": 0
  },
  "ledger": []
}
```

The ledger entry shape is:

```json
{
  "memoryId": "mem-1",
  "action": "create",
  "actor": "local-user",
  "timestamp": 1750000000000,
  "newState": {}
}
```

### 8.3 Retrieval behavior

The retrieval score combines semantic similarity, keyword overlap, tags, domain, entities, layer, recency, and a superseded penalty, then multiplies by confidence. The default threshold is `0.35` and the default top-N is `5`.

The app calls recall with threshold `0.2` and top-N `5`. If a generic recall query returns no strong match, the assistant falls back to recent memories so “What do you remember about me?” still returns stored preferences.

## 9. Feature 4 — World Model event log

### 9.1 What it does

World Model is an append-only event log with derived task entities. `TaskStore` syncs add, toggle, and rename operations through `upsertEntitySync`; deletion appends a tombstone and archives the entity. The Activity panel shows active task entities, event count, recent audit entries, and the last six events.

Relevant files:

- `src/app/services/world-model.service.ts` — app facade, stable entity IDs, persistence.
- `src/app/engines/world-model/` — browser-safe engine port.
- `src/app/components/world-panel/` — Activity panel.

### 9.2 Event model

| Operation | Event kind     | Effect                                                        |
| --------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Add       | `upsertEntity` | Creates an active task entity                                 |
| Toggle    | `upsertEntity` | Updates `completed` and `updatedAt`                           |
| Rename    | `upsertEntity` | Updates `name`, `title`, and `updatedAt`                      |
| Delete    | `tombstone`    | Sets entity state to `archived`; the entity remains in history |
| Merge     | `alias`        | Records an auto-merge; available in the engine API            |
| Ingest    | `upsertEntity`, `relate`, `assertFact` | Used by the ingest pipeline, not the current UI    |

The stable entity ID is derived from `externalId('task', 'todo', task.id)`, so renaming a task does not create a new identity.

## 10. Feature 5 — Markovian plan generation

### 10.1 What it does

Markovian turns a goal into a bounded plan. The app uses a local deterministic `stepFn`, so no model provider is required. Each run records its own `chunkConfig` snapshot, cleans protocol markers from display content, and computes token/efficiency stats.

Relevant files:

- `src/app/services/planning.service.ts` — app facade, history persistence, local generator.
- `src/app/engines/markovian/` — browser-safe engine port.
- `src/app/components/assistant-panel/` — plan output and run metadata.

### 10.2 Plan output

A plan message contains:

- A `Plan for ...` heading.
- Five numbered steps: finish line, moving parts, first three actions, review date, and capture the next action.
- No literal `[DONE]` marker; the marker drives completion and is removed from display content.
- A meta line with the Scout intent, confidence, risk, Markovian run id, and efficiency percentage.

### 10.3 Run record

A `MarkovianRun` includes:

- `id`, `timestamp`, `prompt`, `mode`.
- `chunkConfig` — mandatory per-run snapshot.
- `chunks` — token counts and cleaned content.
- `totalTokensUsed`, `totalTokensSaved`, `efficiencyPercent`.
- `durationMs`, `status`, `tokenLabel`, `output`.
- Optional `reflection` and `error`.

The app config uses `maxChunks: 4`. The local generator completes in one chunk because it emits `[DONE]`.

| MK-08 | Any state                | `Break down the launch into steps`       | Routes to `task.plan` and produces a plan                                       |

### 10.5 Efficiency

`PlanningService.stats()` exposes cumulative history statistics:

- `totalRuns`, `completedRuns`.
- `totalTokensUsed`, `totalTokensSaved`.
- `averageEfficiency`.
- `totalChunksProcessed`, `lastRunTimestamp`.
- `efficiencyHistory`.

Efficiency is recomputed per run against that run’s own `chunkConfig`, never against the current config. This is the key invariant tested by conformance.

## 11. Cross-engine integration scenario

This scenario exercises all four engines in one session.

1. Clear storage: `localStorage.clear(); location.reload();`.
2. Add `Add a task: prepare launch checklist`.
3. Complete it: `Complete prepare launch checklist`.
4. Rename it: `Rename prepare launch checklist to ship launch checklist`.

6. Recall it: `What do you remember about me?`.
7. Plan: `Plan the launch week`.
8. Open the Activity panel and confirm `Task synced` events.
9. Delete the task: `Delete ship launch checklist`, then **Confirm**.
10. Confirm the Activity panel shows `Task archived`.
11. Reload.
12. Confirm:
    - The task is gone.
    - The memory is still present.
    - The World Model event count persists.
    - The Markovian run history persists.

# Meterless Engines Testing Guide

- **Applies to:** `angular-todo-app`
- **Last verified:** 2026-10-23
- **Test runner:** Angular CLI 22 unit-test builder + Vitest 5 + jsdom
- **Engine source:** browser-safe ports under `src/app/engines/`
- **Spec source:** a separate Meterless checkout; commands use `<meterless-spec>` as the placeholder

This guide explains how to verify every user-facing engine feature, what each test proves, how to run the automated suites, how to run the Meterless conformance and eval harnesses, and how to diagnose failures.

---

## 1. Scope

### In scope

- Natural-language assistant actions: add, complete, reopen, rename, delete, filter, list, and summarize tasks.
- Scout Intent routing, clarification, signed execution contracts, prompt-injection blocking, and destructive-action confirmation.
- H-MEM preference memory: remember, recall, forget, persistence, retrieval, and trust-ledger entries.
- World Model event log: task entities, upserts, tombstones, audit entries, and the Activity panel.
- Markovian plan generation: chunk configuration snapshot, marker cleanup, efficiency stats, and history persistence.
- Build, type, template, and CSS-budget verification.

### Out of scope

- Load testing, browser matrix testing, visual regression testing, accessibility certification, and penetration testing.
- Remote model providers. The current assistant is deterministic and local.
- Multi-user concurrency, backend sync, and IndexedDB migration.
- H-MEM dreaming, sleep consolidation, and conflict auto-resolution UI, which exist in the engine API but are not exposed in the app.
- World Model merge-review UI, which records proposals but has no operator screen.

# Angular To-Do App

A small, responsive to-do list built with Angular 22, standalone components, signals, and `localStorage`. No backend, no auth, no extra UI libraries.

The app also ships browser-safe ports of the four Meterless engines: **Scout Intent**, **H-MEM**, **World Model**, and **Markovian**.

## Features

- Add, edit, complete, and delete tasks
- Filter by All, Active, and Completed with live counts
- Remaining-task counter
- Tasks persist across refreshes via `localStorage`
- Empty state for each filter
- Keyboard-friendly editing (`Enter` saves, `Escape` cancels, double-click a title to edit)
- Mobile-responsive layout with a minimal, modern UI
- Natural-language assistant: add, complete, rename, delete, filter, and summarize tasks
- Scout Intent routing with prompt-injection blocking and confirmation for destructive actions
- H-MEM preference memory with retrieval, persistence, and a trust ledger
- World Model event log with task entities and an activity panel
- Markovian plan generation with per-run chunk configuration and efficiency stats

## Run it

```bash
npm install
npm start
```

Open `http://localhost:4200`.

## Verify it

```bash
npm test        # Vitest unit tests
npm run build   # production build
```

See [docs/testing/README.md](docs/testing/README.md) for the full manual and automated testing guide, and [docs/meterless-fit.md](docs/meterless-fit.md) for the implementation map and conformance commands.

## Structure

```text
src/app/
  models/task.model.ts                  Task and filter types
  services/task-store.ts                Signal store, derived views, localStorage
  services/scout.service.ts             Scout Intent facade
  services/memory.service.ts            H-MEM facade and persistence
  services/world-model.service.ts       World Model facade and task sync
  services/planning.service.ts          Markovian facade and persistence
  services/assistant.service.ts         Natural-language action executor
  services/persistence.ts               Shared localStorage JSON helpers
  engines/scout/                        Browser-safe Scout port
  engines/hmem/                         Browser-safe H-MEM port
  engines/world-model/                  Browser-safe World Model port
  engines/markovian/                    Browser-safe Markovian port
  engines/shared/crypto.ts              SHA-256, HMAC, canonical JSON
  directives/autofocus.ts               Focus helper for inline editing
  components/task-input/                Add-task form
  components/task-filters/              All / Active / Completed control
  components/task-item/                 One task row with edit and delete
  components/assistant-panel/           Chat, confirmations, plan output
  components/memory-panel/              Remembered preferences
  components/world-panel/               Event and audit activity
  app.ts / app.html / app.css           Page shell and empty state
```

`TaskStore` remains the only place that mutates tasks. Components are presentational and emit events; derived values (`visibleTasks`, `remainingCount`, `counts`) are `computed` signals. Ordinary CRUD stays on the direct path: component -> `TaskStore` -> `localStorage`.

The assistant path is:

```text
user input
  -> Scout Intent        classify, guard, route
  -> H-MEM               remember or recall preferences
  -> World Model         ground task entities
  -> Markovian           plan long-horizon goals
  -> TaskStore           commit accepted task changes
  -> World Model         append events
```

## Meterless engines

See [docs/meterless-fit.md](docs/meterless-fit.md) for the implementation map, persistence keys, and deliberate limits. See [docs/testing/meterless-engines-testing-guide.md](docs/testing/meterless-engines-testing-guide.md) for detailed test cases and expected results.

Third-party attribution is in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

# Testing

This folder owns the test strategy, commands, and expected results for the app and its Meterless engine ports.

## Start here

- [Meterless Engines Testing Guide](meterless-engines-testing-guide.md) — full manual and automated test guide for the natural-language assistant, Scout Intent, H-MEM, World Model, and Markovian.
- [Meterless Engines implementation map](../meterless-fit.md) — architecture, persistence keys, and engine limits.

## Fast verification

```bash
npm install
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false
npm run build
```

Expected on the current implementation:

- **37 Vitest tests pass** across 7 spec files.
- **Production build succeeds** with no budget errors.
- **Scout eval** passes all thresholds.
- **H-MEM conformance** passes 13/13 checks.
- **World Model conformance** passes 8/8 checks.
- **Markovian conformance** passes 8/8 checks.

## Test layers

| Layer            | Tool                                   | What it proves                                             |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Unit             | Angular CLI unit-test builder + Vitest | Store math, persistence, engine service behavior           |
| Integration      | Angular `TestBed` + jsdom              | Assistant intent -> action -> store -> engine side effects |
| Component        | Angular `TestBed` + jsdom              | App shell and engine panels render                         |
| Conformance      | Meterless runners under `tsx`          | Engine invariants that are independent of this app         |
| Eval             | Scout eval harness under `tsx`         | Intent accuracy, injection recall/precision, tool routing  |
| Production build | Angular AOT build                      | Templates, types, CSS budgets, and bundling                |

## Test data reset

The app persists to `localStorage`. To reset all app state, open DevTools and run:

```js
localStorage.clear();
location.reload();
```

To reset only one subsystem, remove its key:

```js
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.tasks');
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.hmem.v1');
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.world.v1');
localStorage.removeItem('angular-todo-app.markovian.v1');
```

- [Project README](../../README.md)

Spec drop next, see [roadmap](../../ROADMAP.md) | | Quality, cost and latency routing | Runtime | Ships inside Nightshift. Spec drop next, see [roadmap](../../ROADMAP.md) | ## How the engines compose - **H-MEM feeds Markovian.** Memory seeds chunk zero of a long run and mines the output back into memory. The [memory-compounding demo](../../examples/memory-compounding-research/) shows the warm run finishing in 8 chunks instead of 12. - **World Model feeds H-MEM.** Sourced facts replicate into memory and answer scoped queries planned upstream. - **Scout plans before anything acts.** Downstream engines act only on its signed execution contracts. - **Markovian is the `deliberate` job kind.** In Nightshift, one long chain of chunks carries a compressed summary forward and checkpoints. - **All three together make a small model feel large.** Meterless City runs an 8B model with Markovian state, H-MEM memory and a World Model event log per character. Each engine's examples folder shows these pairings from its own side. ## Product surfaces | Surface | Role | Docs | |---|---|---| | Nightshift | The flagship: AI hotspot by day, overnight production by night | [docs/products/nightshift/](../products/nightshift/README.md) | | Gaia | Persistent workspace | [docs/products/gaia/](../products/gaia/README.md) | | Relay | Repeatable desktop workflows | [docs/products/relay/](../products/relay/README.md) | | Swarms | Coordinated, divergent generation | [docs/products/swarms/](../products/swarms/README.md) | | Experiments | What the runtime unlocks | [docs/experiments/](../experiments/README.md) | === markovian-with-hmem === # Markovian with H-MEM > Run it: `npx tsx index.ts` (uses the reference implementation in [`../../reference`](../../reference)). > **Marker note:** this walkthrough uses the XML alternate (``, ``) of the canonical bracket protocol (`[STATE_CHECKPOINT]` / `[TASK_COMPLETE]`). See [docs/marker-protocol.md](../../docs/marker-protocol.md) for the 1:1 mapping. [H-MEM](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem) feeds chunk zero with relevant prior memories, and the final run output is mined back into memory. Today's long run then informs next week's. > Memory enters at step 1 only. After that, bounded carryover maintains continuity. H-MEM is not re-queried every chunk. Prerequisite reading: [`docs/architecture.md`](../../docs/architecture.md), and the `01-add-memory` example in the [H-MEM engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem). --- ## The contract (from the how-to §13) ```text hmem.query ─▶ formatReinjection ─▶ memoryContext ─▶ Markovian chunk 0 ONLY │ ▼ run completes → hmem.ingest("plan_completion") ``` Heavy context enters once; the compressed carryover carries continuity forward. The completed run becomes a new memory for future runs. ## Walkthrough: `index.ts` ```ts import { Markovian } from "@meterless/markovian"; import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem"; const hmem = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "agent-cleo" }); const markovian = new Markovian({ chunkConfig: { chunkSize: 6000, carryoverTokens: 900 } }); const userPrompt = "Plan the Q3 analytics-warehouse migration."; // 1. Pull relevant memory BEFORE the run (past decisions, constraints, prefs). const { memories } = await hmem.query({ text: userPrompt, topN: 5 }); const memoryContext = formatReinjection(memories); // → "[infra] (long_term) Team standardized on AWS Glue catalog. {entities: Glue}\n..." // 2. Inject it into chunk ZERO only via memoryContext. const run = await markovian.run({ goal: userPrompt, memoryContext, // engine prepends this to step 1's prompt only stepFn: myStepFn, stopWhen: ({ output }) => output.includes(""), }); // 3. Mine the completed run back into H-MEM as a durable memory. await hmem.ingest({ eventType: "plan_completion", source: `markovian:${run.id}`, content: run.chunks.map((c) => c.content).join("\n\n"), }); console.log(run.output); ``` ## Run it ```bash # No npm package is published. This repo is an implementation spec. # Point the imports at your implementations of the engine contracts (see ../../AGENTS.md), then: npx tsx ./index.ts ``` ## Expected behavior ```text hmem.query → 5 memories (incl. "Team standardized on AWS Glue catalog") chunk 0 prompt includes that memory → the plan picks Glue WITHOUT re-deciding it chunks 1..N → bounded carryover only (memory NOT re-injected) run completes → hmem.ingest stores the plan as a plan_completion memory next week: a new migration run's hmem.query surfaces THIS plan as prior context ``` ## The closing loop | Phase | Engine | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | Before | H-MEM `query` | retrieves the Glue-catalog decision from a past run | | Chunk 0 | Markovian | the plan inherits that decision instead of re-litigating it | | Chunks 1..N | Markovian | carryover only; flat cost preserved | | After | H-MEM `ingest` | this plan becomes memory for the next planning run | --- ## Why it matters - **Memory enters at chunk zero only.** Re-injecting H-MEM every chunk would defeat the O(1) property, because the prompt would grow with retrieved memory each step. The contract (`memoryContext` → step 1 only) keeps Markovian flat and memory-aware. - **The two engines have complementary jobs.** H-MEM decides what past knowledge is relevant. Markovian decides how to reason through a long task without re-paying for it. Neither does the other's job. - **The loop makes long-horizon work cumulative.** A plan that ignores last quarter's decisions repeats them. `ingest("plan_completion")` lets the agent build on its earlier runs. ## Next - The `markovian-handoff` example in the [H-MEM engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem): the same loop, seen from inside H-MEM. - [`markovian-inside-swarm`](../markovian-inside-swarm/README.md): the other composition seam. - H-MEM's reinjection model: [H-MEM](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem). === hmem markovian-handoff === # Markovian handoff > Cross-engine example: this folder has no runnable code yet. Treat the code below as a reference sketch of the contract. H-MEM is the memory a long [Markovian](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian) run starts from and writes back to. This example is the H-MEM side of the loop: what `query` serves into chunk zero, and what `ingest` absorbs when the run completes. > The reciprocal example, `markovian-with-hmem`, lives in the [Markovian engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian). It focuses on the chunked run; this one focuses on the memory contract feeding and closing it. Prerequisite reading: [`04-retrieve-and-reinject`](../04-retrieve-and-reinject/README.md), [`docs/reinjection.md`](../../docs/reinjection.md). --- ## The loop, from memory's side ```text hmem.query ──serves──▶ memoryContext ──▶ Markovian chunk 0 (once, never re-queried) │ ▼ run completes hmem.ingest("plan_completion") ◀──absorbs── joined chunk content ``` H-MEM does two things and nothing else here: retrieve the relevant prior decisions before the run, and mine the finished run back as a durable memory. ## Walkthrough (illustrative reference API) The code below is a reference sketch of the contract, not a runnable package. This repo is the implementation spec, and no `@meterless/*` npm packages are published. The `@meterless/hmem` and `@meterless/markovian` imports stand for your own implementations. ```ts import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem"; import { Markovian } from "@meterless/markovian"; const hmem = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "agent-cleo" }); const prompt = "Plan the Q3 analytics-warehouse migration."; // 1. Memory's job #1: retrieve what past runs already decided. const { memories } = await hmem.query({ text: prompt, topN: 5 }); // → [ "[infra] (long_term) Team standardized on AWS Glue catalog. {entities: Glue}", ... ] const markovian = new Markovian({ chunkConfig: { chunkSize: 6000, carryoverTokens: 900 } }); const run = await markovian.run({ goal: prompt, memoryContext: formatReinjection(memories), // enters chunk 0 ONLY skipSemanticMemoryAugmentation: true, // lower layers must NOT retrieve a second time stepFn: myStepFn, stopWhen: ({ output }) => output.includes("[TASK_COMPLETE]"), }); // 2. Memory's job #2: absorb the completed run as a new durable memory. await hmem.ingest({ eventType: "plan_completion", source: `markovian:${run.id}`, content: run.chunks.map((c) => c.content).join("\n\n"), }); // Prove the loop closed: the new memory is now retrievable. const next = await hmem.query({ text: "warehouse migration plan", topN: 1 }); console.log(next.memories[0].source); // → "markovian:" ``` ## Expected behavior (illustrative) ```text hmem.query → 5 memories (incl. the Glue-catalog decision from a prior run) markovian → plan inherits Glue WITHOUT re-deciding it (memory in chunk 0) hmem.ingest → run stored as a plan_completion memory, source=markovian: hmem.query → next migration question now surfaces THIS plan as prior context ``` ## What `ingest("plan_completion")` actually does | Step | H-MEM behavior | | --- | --- | | receive run content | classified as a `plan_completion` event | | mine | extract durable facts/decisions, not the raw transcript | | enrich | domain, entities, `source: markovian:` provenance | | store | written to the working tier, audited in the trust ledger | | later | eligible for retrieval, dreaming, and sleep like any memory | The completed Markovian run does not get dumped verbatim. It is mined the same way a chat or document is (see [`02-mine-from-chat`](../02-mine-from-chat/README.md)). --- ## Why it matters - **H-MEM makes long runs cumulative.** Markovian gives flat per-step cost; H-MEM is what stops the next run from re-deciding what this one already settled. Without the `ingest` step, every migration plan starts from zero. - **Retrieval feeds chunk zero, not every chunk.** H-MEM serves context once. Re-injecting per chunk would defeat Markovian's O(1) property. The memory contract respects the engine boundary on purpose. That is also why `skipSemanticMemoryAugmentation: true` is passed down: a chunked generator whose lower layer also auto-augments prompts with memory would retrieve twice. - **The handoff is provenanced both ways.** What entered the run is a `query` trace; what left it is a `plan_completion` memory tagged `markovian:`. The full round trip is auditable from the ledger. ## Next - `markovian-with-hmem` in the [Markovian engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian): the reciprocal view, the same loop from inside Markovian. - [`world-model-sync`](../world-model-sync/README.md): the other "memory absorbs an external engine" pattern. - [`02-mine-from-chat`](../02-mine-from-chat/README.md: how `ingest` mines durable memory from raw content.

=== scout query hmem ===
# Query H-MEM before action

Scout's Interpret stage does not decide in a vacuum. It emits a context plan telling [H-MEM](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem) how aggressively to retrieve, then folds the returned memories back into intent confidence and tool selection. The decision is grounded in the user's history, preferences, and prior corrections.

Prerequisite reading: [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md), the [H-MEM engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem).

---

## Scenario

```text
"draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire"
```

"the usual" is unrecoverable without memory. Scout must pull the user's prior onboarding-email preferences from H-MEM before it can confidently classify and plan.

---

## Walkthrough: `index.ts`

```ts
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";
import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem";

const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });
const hmem  = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "user-u1" });

// 1. Scout emits a CONTEXT PLAN: it decides how aggressive retrieval should be.
const plan = await scout.planContext({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" },
  surface: "chat",
});
console.log(plan.contextPlan);
// { sources: ["memory"], maxTokens: 4000, redactionPolicy: "default_internal" }

// 2. Execute the plan against H-MEM (plan drives topN + strategy).
const wantsMemory = plan.contextPlan.sources.includes("memory");
const { memories } = await hmem.query({
  text: "draft the usual onboarding email",
  topN: wantsMemory ? 8 : 0,
  strategy: plan.contextPlan.redactionPolicy === "default_internal" ? "comprehensive" : "minimal",
});

// 3. Decide WITH the retrieved memory folded in.
const decision = await scout.decide({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" },
  surface: "chat",
  context: memories,
});

console.log("intent:", decision.intent.primary.id, decision.intent.primary.confidence);
console.log("params:", decision.intent.parameters);
```

## Run it

```bash
# No @meterless package is published. @meterless/scout names your own
# spec-conforming implementation. With it on your import path:
npx tsx ./index.ts
```

## Expected output

```text
{ sources: ["memory"], maxTokens: 4000, redactionPolicy: "default_internal" }
hmem.query → 3 memories (incl. "prefers warm tone, includes 30-60-90 plan link")
intent: email.draft 0.93     ← confidence rose: "the usual" disambiguated by memory
params: { tone: "warm", template: "onboarding-v3", include: ["30-60-90-plan"] }
```

## How memory changed the decision

| Without memory | With memory (this example) |
| --- | --- |
| "the usual" → ambiguous → `email.draft` at 0.61 (**medium** → clarify) | resolved → `email.draft` at 0.93 (**high** → proceed) |
| no parameters; would have to ask the user | `tone`, `template`, `include` filled from prior corrections |
| generic email | the user's established onboarding email |

The contextual term in the scoring formula (`0.20 · contextual`) is where retrieved memory lifts confidence. A medium-band guess becomes a high-band decision because the history grounded it.

## Scout decides the retrieval budget

```text
trivial lookup           → contextPlan.sources = []        → topN 0  (don't pay for memory)
"the usual" / references → contextPlan.sources = ["memory"] → topN 8, comprehensive
sensitive surface        → redactionPolicy tightens          → strategy "minimal"
```

H-MEM does not guess how hard to search. Scout's context plan tells it. Retrieval aggressiveness is an intent-layer decision, recorded on the contract.

---

## Why it matters

- **"The usual" only works with grounded memory.** Reference-laden prompts are unrecoverable from text alone. Pulling history before deciding turns an ambiguous clarify-loop into a confident one-shot.
- **Scout sizes the retrieval, not the memory store.** A trivial prompt should not drag 8 memories into the decision; a referential one must. The context plan makes that an explicit, auditable choice instead of a fixed default.
- **Memory raises confidence traceably.** It feeds the contextual scoring term, so a medium→high band shift traces to specific retrieved memories.

## Next

- The reciprocal view, the same call from inside H-MEM, lives in the [H-MEM engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem).
- [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md): the contract this grounded decision seals.

# Scout-grounded recall

> Cross-engine example: the scout-intent spec is published (see [`engines/scout-intent/`](../../../scout-intent/)); this runs once a Scout reference implementation lands. Until then treat the code as a reference sketch of the contract.

Before [Scout Intent](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/scout-intent) decides what to do, it asks H-MEM what the agent already knows. This example is the H-MEM side: how a Scout context plan maps to a retrieval call, and what the returned memories carry that lets Scout decide confidently instead of guessing.

> The reciprocal example, `query-hmem-before-action`, lives in the [Scout Intent engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/scout-intent). It focuses on Scout folding memory into intent confidence; this one focuses on what H-MEM serves and why.

Prerequisite reading: [`04-retrieve-and-reinject`](../04-retrieve-and-reinject/README.md), [`docs/retrieval-ranking.md`](../../docs/retrieval-ranking.md).

---

## Scenario

```text
"draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire"
```

"the usual" is unrecoverable from the prompt alone. Scout cannot confidently classify it until H-MEM returns the user's prior onboarding-email preferences and corrections.

## The contract, from memory's side

```text
Scout context plan { sources:["memory"], redactionPolicy:"default_internal" }
        │  Scout decides HOW aggressive retrieval should be
        ▼
hmem.query({ topN, strategy })   ← H-MEM decides WHAT comes back
        │  ranked, trace-tagged memories
        ▼
Scout.decide(context = memories) ← confidence rises on the contextual signal
```

## Walkthrough (illustrative reference API)

The code below is a reference sketch of the contract, not a runnable package. This repo is the implementation spec, and no `@meterless/*` npm packages are published. The `@meterless/hmem` and `@meterless/scout` imports stand for your own implementations.

```ts
import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem";
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";

const hmem  = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "user-u1" });
const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });

// Scout sizes the retrieval; it does not do the retrieving.
const plan = await scout.planContext({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" }, surface: "chat",
});

// H-MEM answers the plan. Plan → topN + strategy mapping:
const { memories, trace } = await hmem.query({
  text: "draft the usual onboarding email",
  topN: plan.contextPlan.sources.includes("memory") ? 8 : 0,
  strategy: plan.contextPlan.redactionPolicy === "default_internal" ? "comprehensive" : "minimal",
});

for (const m of memories) console.log(`${m.type}  ${m.content}  ←${m.source}`);
console.log("retrieval reason:", trace.retrievalReason);

// Scout decides WITH what memory returned.
const decision = await scout.decide({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" }, surface: "chat",
  context: memories,
});
console.log("intent:", decision.intent.primary.id, decision.intent.primary.confidence);
```

## Expected output (illustrative)

```text
preference  Onboarding emails use a warm tone, include the 30-60-90 plan link  ←feedback:correction
preference  Template onboarding-v3, CC the new hire's manager                  ←session:s-204
factual     Last onboarding email was sent 2026-04-30                           ←event:email_sent
retrieval reason: domain+entity match on "onboarding email"; comprehensive (default_internal)
intent: email.draft 0.93
```

## What H-MEM contributes to the decision

| H-MEM returns | Effect on Scout |
| --- | --- |
| 3 ranked memories with `trace.retrievalReason` | the `0.20·contextual` term in scoring lifts confidence 0.61 → 0.93 |
| `type: preference` records from prior corrections | `email.draft` parameters fill in (tone, template), with no clarify loop |
| `source:` provenance on each | Scout's contract can cite why it inferred "the usual" |

H-MEM does not decide the intent. It supplies grounded, provenanced recall so Scout's existing scoring resolves a medium-band guess into a high-band decision. The retrieval strategy (`comprehensive` vs `minimal`) is dictated by Scout's plan, not chosen by H-MEM.

---

## Why it matters

- **Scout sizes the recall; H-MEM serves it.** A trivial prompt yields `topN: 0`, so memory is not consulted. A reference-laden one ("the usual") gets a comprehensive pull. The split keeps retrieval cost proportional to ambiguity.
- **The trace is what makes the decision auditable.** `trace.retrievalReason` rides into Scout's contract, so "why did Scout think this was `email.draft`?" traces back to specific memories and their `source:` provenance.
- **Memory raises confidence through attributable records.** It feeds Scout's contextual scoring term: a medium→high band shift attributable to named records, not an opaque bump.

## Next

- `query-hmem-before-action` in the [Scout Intent engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/scout-intent): the reciprocal view, the same call from inside Scout.
- [`04-retrieve-and-reinject`](../04-retrieve-and-reinject/README.md): the retrieval + trace mechanics in depth.
- [`world-model-sync`](../world-model-sync/README.md) · [`markovian-handoff`](../markovian-handoff/README.md): H-MEM's other integration seams.

# Route to Markovian

Scout sits above every other engine. When it detects a long-horizon task, it does not run it. It emits a contract that routes to the [Markovian Engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian) for bounded-context reasoning, and Markovian verifies that contract before it starts.

Prerequisite reading: [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md), the [Markovian Engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian).

---

## Scenario

```text
"Plan our 6-month analytics-warehouse migration to Iceberg."
```

This is `architecture.plan`, an intent that declares `markovian.chain` as a capability. It takes 15+ reasoning steps; a single model call cannot do it justice.

---

## Walkthrough: `index.ts`

```ts
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";
import { Markovian } from "@meterless/markovian";

const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });

// 1. Scout decides. It does NOT reason about the migration itself.
const decision = await scout.decide({
  prompt: "Plan our 6-month analytics-warehouse migration to Iceberg.",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "architect" },
  surface: "chat",
});

console.log(decision.intent.primary.id);   // "architecture.plan"
console.log(decision.toolPlan);            // [{ tool: "markovian.chain", reason: "long-horizon" }]

// 2. The contract is the handoff. Markovian verifies it BEFORE running.
const markovian = new Markovian({ chunkConfig: { tokensPerChunk: 6000, carryoverTokens: 800 } });

const run = await markovian.runFromContract(decision.executionContract, {
  secret: process.env.SCOUT_SECRET,           // verify signature + expiry first
  stepFn: myArchitectStepFn,
  stopWhen: ({ output }) => output.includes("[TASK_COMPLETE]"),
});

console.log(`${run.chunks.length} chunks · ${run.stats.efficiency}% saved`);
```

## Run it

```bash
# No @meterless package is published. @meterless/scout names your own
# spec-conforming implementation. With it on your import path:
npx tsx ./index.ts
```

## Expected output

```text
architecture.plan
[ { tool: "markovian.chain", reason: "long-horizon decision-heavy task" } ]
markovian: contract verified (sig ok, not expired, capability markovian.chain in scope)
15 chunks · 86% saved
```

## How Scout decides "this is long-horizon"

```text
intent architecture.plan declares capability markovian.chain
        +
estimated-steps heuristic / intent metadata says "decision-heavy, multi-phase"
        ↓
toolPlan = [markovian.chain]
modelProfile = high_reasoning
        ↓
execution contract scoped to capability "markovian.chain" only
```

Scout never sees the migration content. It classifies the shape of the work and routes accordingly. The reasoning happens entirely inside Markovian's bounded chunks.

## The handoff is the contract, nothing else

```text
Scout ──signed contract──▶ Markovian
                              │ verifyContract(): sig ok? not expired? markovian.chain in scope?
                              │   any check fails → refused at the boundary
                              ▼
                       bounded chunked run (Scout never re-consulted per chunk)
```

Long runs that need more time call `scout.replan({ parent })` for a fresh contract on the same `traceId`. They do not extend the original contract's TTL.

---

## Why it matters

- **Scout decides; Markovian reasons.** The two are kept separate: intent/risk/routing live in Scout, bounded long-horizon execution lives in Markovian. Neither re-implements the other.
- **The contract gates the engine.** Markovian refuses to start on an unsigned, expired, or out-of-scope contract. The same property that makes every Scout handoff auditable applies to the long-horizon path.
- **Routing is on shape, not content.** Scout flags "this is long and decision-heavy" without reading the migration plan. That is what keeps the decision layer cheap and the reasoning layer where it belongs.

=== scout to world model ===
# Scout to World Model

When a decision needs grounding in shared state, Scout does not let the agent free-roam the [World Model](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/world-model). It emits a scoped context plan (how broad a slice, which relations, what budget), and the world's read surface answers exactly that. The agent only reasons over what it is handed.

> This is the Scout side of the World Model's context-plan integration. The World Model repo shows the world answering the plan; this example shows Scout issuing it.

Prerequisite reading: [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md), the [World Model repo](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/world-model).

---

## The idea

> Scout owns intent → context plan. The World Model owns plan → context. The agent reasons; it never navigates the graph itself.

A vague prompt and a strategic one should pull different amounts of world. Scout decides the breadth from the intent; the world honors it.

## Walkthrough: `index.ts`

```ts
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";
import { WorldModel } from "@meterless/world-model";

const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });
const world = new WorldModel({ storage: "local", namespace: "scout-demo" });

async function answer(prompt: string) {
  // 1. Scout produces a context plan sized to the intent (NOT a fixed default).
  const plan = await scout.planContext({
    prompt, user: { id: "u-1", role: "ae" }, surface: "chat",
  });
  console.log(plan.contextPlan);
  // { subjectId: "account:salesforce:0015g00000ACME",
  //   sources: ["world"], maxTokens: 6000, relations: ["employs","has-deal"] }

  // 2. The plan becomes a read-surface query. The agent wrote none of this.
  const wide = plan.contextPlan.maxTokens > 16_000;
  const context = await world.buildPromptContext({
    subjectId: plan.contextPlan.subjectId,
    limit: wide ? 50 : 20,
    include: plan.contextPlan.relations,
    window: { start: Date.now() - 7 * 86_400_000, end: Date.now() },
  });

  // 3. Scout decides WITH the assembled, provenanced context.
  const decision = await scout.decide({
    prompt, user: { id: "u-1", role: "ae" }, surface: "chat",
    context: context.text,
  });
  return { intent: decision.intent.primary, entities: context.provenance.length };
}

const quick = await answer("what's Acme's primary contact?");
const deep  = await answer("build a full account plan for Acme next quarter");
console.log(quick.entities, "vs", deep.entities);
```

## Run it

```bash
# No @meterless package is published. @meterless/scout names your own
# spec-conforming implementation. With it on your import path:
npx tsx ./index.ts
```

## Expected output

```text
{ subjectId: "account:salesforce:0015g00000ACME", sources: ["world"], maxTokens: 6000, relations: ["employs","has-deal"] }
6 vs 41
```

Same world, same subject. The quick lookup pulled a tight neighborhood (≤20 → 6 entities). The account-planning prompt produced a wide plan (≤50 → 41), so Scout asked the world for far more context, automatically, from the intent.

## What Scout puts on the contract

| Field | Set by | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `contextPlan.subjectId` | intent + entity binding | which world node to center the query on |
| `contextPlan.sources` | intent risk/class | `["world"]` vs `[]` (skip retrieval entirely) |
| `contextPlan.maxTokens` | intent breadth | the read surface's `limit` |
| `contextPlan.relations` | intent capability map | which edges to traverse |

The plan is part of the signed execution contract, so "why did the agent see these 41 entities?" traces back to a specific Scout decision instead of an ad-hoc query.

---

## Why it matters

- **The agent never navigates the world.** It writes no graph traversal and picks no budget. Scout plans; the read surface executes; the agent only reasons over the result.
- **Context scales with intent.** A trivial question does not drag 50 entities into the prompt; a strategic one is not starved at 20. Breadth is a Scout decision recorded on the contract.
- **Provenance survives the whole path.** The assembled context returns the rows that produced it, traceable back through Scout's plan to the World Model events in one auditable chain.

<skill_content name="planning-artifact-naming">
# Skill: planning-artifact-naming

# Planning Artifact Naming Convention (v1)

This skill defines the naming convention for all planning artifacts
generated during AI-agent sessions. The convention embeds session
identity (human-readable name + machine-readable ID) directly into
each filename, ensuring artifacts are self-traceable to their source
conversation and sort chronologically at the filesystem level.

The convention was established during an OpenCode config preservation
session and generalised here for reuse across all agent workflows.

***

## 1. Formula

```text
docs/<date>_<session-id>_<session-name-slug>_<artifact-type>_v<version>.md
```

All planning artifacts MUST be stored under `docs/` in the main
repository (per
[Traceability Portability Mandate](../../../../../ai-agent-rules/ai-rule-standardization-rules.md)).

### 1.1 Part Reference

| Part | Required | Format | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `date` | Always | `YYYY-MM-DD` | `2026-07-03` |
| `session-id` | Always | Full opencode session ID (without `ses_` prefix) | `<session-id>` |
| `session-name-slug` | Always | Kebab-case of the opencode session name | `opencode-config-versioning-preservation` |
