=== scout query hmem ===
# Query H-MEM before action

Scout's Interpret stage does not decide in a vacuum. It emits a context plan telling [H-MEM](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem) how aggressively to retrieve, then folds the returned memories back into intent confidence and tool selection. The decision is grounded in the user's history, preferences, and prior corrections.

Prerequisite reading: [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md), the [H-MEM engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem).

---

## Scenario

```text
"draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire"
```

"the usual" is unrecoverable without memory. Scout must pull the user's prior onboarding-email preferences from H-MEM before it can confidently classify and plan.

---

## Walkthrough: `index.ts`

```ts
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";
import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem";

const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });
const hmem  = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "user-u1" });

// 1. Scout emits a CONTEXT PLAN: it decides how aggressive retrieval should be.
const plan = await scout.planContext({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" },
  surface: "chat",
});
console.log(plan.contextPlan);
// { sources: ["memory"], maxTokens: 4000, redactionPolicy: "default_internal" }

// 2. Execute the plan against H-MEM (plan drives topN + strategy).
const wantsMemory = plan.contextPlan.sources.includes("memory");
const { memories } = await hmem.query({
  text: "draft the usual onboarding email",
  topN: wantsMemory ? 8 : 0,
  strategy: plan.contextPlan.redactionPolicy === "default_internal" ? "comprehensive" : "minimal",
});

// 3. Decide WITH the retrieved memory folded in.
const decision = await scout.decide({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" },
  surface: "chat",
  context: memories,
});

console.log("intent:", decision.intent.primary.id, decision.intent.primary.confidence);
console.log("params:", decision.intent.parameters);
```

## Run it

```bash
# No @meterless package is published. @meterless/scout names your own
# spec-conforming implementation. With it on your import path:
npx tsx ./index.ts
```

## Expected output

```text
{ sources: ["memory"], maxTokens: 4000, redactionPolicy: "default_internal" }
hmem.query → 3 memories (incl. "prefers warm tone, includes 30-60-90 plan link")
intent: email.draft 0.93     ← confidence rose: "the usual" disambiguated by memory
params: { tone: "warm", template: "onboarding-v3", include: ["30-60-90-plan"] }
```

## How memory changed the decision

| Without memory | With memory (this example) |
| --- | --- |
| "the usual" → ambiguous → `email.draft` at 0.61 (**medium** → clarify) | resolved → `email.draft` at 0.93 (**high** → proceed) |
| no parameters; would have to ask the user | `tone`, `template`, `include` filled from prior corrections |
| generic email | the user's established onboarding email |

The contextual term in the scoring formula (`0.20 · contextual`) is where retrieved memory lifts confidence. A medium-band guess becomes a high-band decision because the history grounded it.

## Scout decides the retrieval budget

```text
trivial lookup           → contextPlan.sources = []        → topN 0  (don't pay for memory)
"the usual" / references → contextPlan.sources = ["memory"] → topN 8, comprehensive
sensitive surface        → redactionPolicy tightens          → strategy "minimal"
```

H-MEM does not guess how hard to search. Scout's context plan tells it. Retrieval aggressiveness is an intent-layer decision, recorded on the contract.

---

## Why it matters

- **"The usual" only works with grounded memory.** Reference-laden prompts are unrecoverable from text alone. Pulling history before deciding turns an ambiguous clarify-loop into a confident one-shot.
- **Scout sizes the retrieval, not the memory store.** A trivial prompt should not drag 8 memories into the decision; a referential one must. The context plan makes that an explicit, auditable choice instead of a fixed default.
- **Memory raises confidence traceably.** It feeds the contextual scoring term, so a medium→high band shift traces to specific retrieved memories.

## Next

- The reciprocal view, the same call from inside H-MEM, lives in the [H-MEM engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem).
- [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md): the contract this grounded decision seals.

=== hmem scout grounded recall ===
# Scout-grounded recall

> Cross-engine example: the scout-intent spec is published (see [`engines/scout-intent/`](../../../scout-intent/)); this runs once a Scout reference implementation lands. Until then treat the code as a reference sketch of the contract.

Before [Scout Intent](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/scout-intent) decides what to do, it asks H-MEM what the agent already knows. This example is the H-MEM side: how a Scout context plan maps to a retrieval call, and what the returned memories carry that lets Scout decide confidently instead of guessing.

> The reciprocal example, `query-hmem-before-action`, lives in the [Scout Intent engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/scout-intent). It focuses on Scout folding memory into intent confidence; this one focuses on what H-MEM serves and why.

Prerequisite reading: [`04-retrieve-and-reinject`](../04-retrieve-and-reinject/README.md), [`docs/retrieval-ranking.md`](../../docs/retrieval-ranking.md).

---

## Scenario

```text
"draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire"
```

"the usual" is unrecoverable from the prompt alone. Scout cannot confidently classify it until H-MEM returns the user's prior onboarding-email preferences and corrections.

## The contract, from memory's side

```text
Scout context plan { sources:["memory"], redactionPolicy:"default_internal" }
        │  Scout decides HOW aggressive retrieval should be
        ▼
hmem.query({ topN, strategy })   ← H-MEM decides WHAT comes back
        │  ranked, trace-tagged memories
        ▼
Scout.decide(context = memories) ← confidence rises on the contextual signal
```

## Walkthrough (illustrative reference API)

The code below is a reference sketch of the contract, not a runnable package. This repo is the implementation spec, and no `@meterless/*` npm packages are published. The `@meterless/hmem` and `@meterless/scout` imports stand for your own implementations.

```ts
import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem";
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";

const hmem  = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "user-u1" });
const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });

// Scout sizes the retrieval; it does not do the retrieving.
const plan = await scout.planContext({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" }, surface: "chat",
});

// H-MEM answers the plan. Plan → topN + strategy mapping:
const { memories, trace } = await hmem.query({
  text: "draft the usual onboarding email",
  topN: plan.contextPlan.sources.includes("memory") ? 8 : 0,
  strategy: plan.contextPlan.redactionPolicy === "default_internal" ? "comprehensive" : "minimal",
});

for (const m of memories) console.log(`${m.type}  ${m.content}  ←${m.source}`);
console.log("retrieval reason:", trace.retrievalReason);

// Scout decides WITH what memory returned.
const decision = await scout.decide({
  prompt: "draft the usual onboarding email for the new hire",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "manager" }, surface: "chat",
  context: memories,
});
console.log("intent:", decision.intent.primary.id, decision.intent.primary.confidence);
```

## Expected output (illustrative)

```text
preference  Onboarding emails use a warm tone, include the 30-60-90 plan link  ←feedback:correction
preference  Template onboarding-v3, CC the new hire's manager                  ←session:s-204
factual     Last onboarding email was sent 2026-04-30                           ←event:email_sent
retrieval reason: domain+entity match on "onboarding email"; comprehensive (default_internal)
intent: email.draft 0.93
```

## What H-MEM contributes to the decision

| H-MEM returns | Effect on Scout |
| --- | --- |
| 3 ranked memories with `trace.retrievalReason` | the `0.20·contextual` term in scoring lifts confidence 0.61 → 0.93 |
| `type: preference` records from prior corrections | `email.draft` parameters fill in (tone, template), with no clarify loop |
| `source:` provenance on each | Scout's contract can cite why it inferred "the usual" |

H-MEM does not decide the intent. It supplies grounded, provenanced recall so Scout's existing scoring resolves a medium-band guess into a high-band decision. The retrieval strategy (`comprehensive` vs `minimal`) is dictated by Scout's plan, not chosen by H-MEM.

---

## Why it matters

- **Scout sizes the recall; H-MEM serves it.** A trivial prompt yields `topN: 0`, so memory is not consulted. A reference-laden one ("the usual") gets a comprehensive pull. The split keeps retrieval cost proportional to ambiguity.
- **The trace is what makes the decision auditable.** `trace.retrievalReason` rides into Scout's contract, so "why did Scout think this was `email.draft`?" traces back to specific memories and their `source:` provenance.
- **Memory raises confidence through attributable records.** It feeds Scout's contextual scoring term: a medium→high band shift attributable to named records, not an opaque bump.

## Next

- `query-hmem-before-action` in the [Scout Intent engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/scout-intent): the reciprocal view, the same call from inside Scout.
- [`04-retrieve-and-reinject`](../04-retrieve-and-reinject/README.md): the retrieval + trace mechanics in depth.
- [`world-model-sync`](../world-model-sync/README.md) · [`markovian-handoff`](../markovian-handoff/README.md): H-MEM's other integration seams.

=== scout route markovian ===
# Route to Markovian

Scout sits above every other engine. When it detects a long-horizon task, it does not run it. It emits a contract that routes to the [Markovian Engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian) for bounded-context reasoning, and Markovian verifies that contract before it starts.

Prerequisite reading: [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md), the [Markovian Engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian).

---

## Scenario

```text
"Plan our 6-month analytics-warehouse migration to Iceberg."
```

This is `architecture.plan`, an intent that declares `markovian.chain` as a capability. It takes 15+ reasoning steps; a single model call cannot do it justice.

---

## Walkthrough: `index.ts`

```ts
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";
import { Markovian } from "@meterless/markovian";

const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });

// 1. Scout decides. It does NOT reason about the migration itself.
const decision = await scout.decide({
  prompt: "Plan our 6-month analytics-warehouse migration to Iceberg.",
  user: { id: "u-1", role: "architect" },
  surface: "chat",
});

console.log(decision.intent.primary.id);   // "architecture.plan"
console.log(decision.toolPlan);            // [{ tool: "markovian.chain", reason: "long-horizon" }]

// 2. The contract is the handoff. Markovian verifies it BEFORE running.
const markovian = new Markovian({ chunkConfig: { tokensPerChunk: 6000, carryoverTokens: 800 } });

const run = await markovian.runFromContract(decision.executionContract, {
  secret: process.env.SCOUT_SECRET,           // verify signature + expiry first
  stepFn: myArchitectStepFn,
  stopWhen: ({ output }) => output.includes("[TASK_COMPLETE]"),
});

console.log(`${run.chunks.length} chunks · ${run.stats.efficiency}% saved`);
```

## Run it

```bash
# No @meterless package is published. @meterless/scout names your own
# spec-conforming implementation. With it on your import path:
npx tsx ./index.ts
```

## Expected output

```text
architecture.plan
[ { tool: "markovian.chain", reason: "long-horizon decision-heavy task" } ]
markovian: contract verified (sig ok, not expired, capability markovian.chain in scope)
15 chunks · 86% saved
```

## How Scout decides "this is long-horizon"

```text
intent architecture.plan declares capability markovian.chain
        +
estimated-steps heuristic / intent metadata says "decision-heavy, multi-phase"
        ↓
toolPlan = [markovian.chain]
modelProfile = high_reasoning
        ↓
execution contract scoped to capability "markovian.chain" only
```

Scout never sees the migration content. It classifies the shape of the work and routes accordingly. The reasoning happens entirely inside Markovian's bounded chunks.

## The handoff is the contract, nothing else

```text
Scout ──signed contract──▶ Markovian
                              │ verifyContract(): sig ok? not expired? markovian.chain in scope?
                              │   any check fails → refused at the boundary
                              ▼
                       bounded chunked run (Scout never re-consulted per chunk)
```

Long runs that need more time call `scout.replan({ parent })` for a fresh contract on the same `traceId`. They do not extend the original contract's TTL.

---

## Why it matters

- **Scout decides; Markovian reasons.** The two are kept separate: intent/risk/routing live in Scout, bounded long-horizon execution lives in Markovian. Neither re-implements the other.
- **The contract gates the engine.** Markovian refuses to start on an unsigned, expired, or out-of-scope contract. The same property that makes every Scout handoff auditable applies to the long-horizon path.
- **Routing is on shape, not content.** Scout flags "this is long and decision-heavy" without reading the migration plan. That is what keeps the decision layer cheap and the reasoning layer where it belongs.

## Next

- [`scout-to-swarm`](../scout-to-swarm/README.md): the parallel-specialists handoff.
- Markovian's view of long-horizon work: the [Markovian engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian).

=== scout to world model ===
# Scout to World Model

When a decision needs grounding in shared state, Scout does not let the agent free-roam the [World Model](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/world-model). It emits a scoped context plan (how broad a slice, which relations, what budget), and the world's read surface answers exactly that. The agent only reasons over what it is handed.

> This is the Scout side of the World Model's context-plan integration. The World Model repo shows the world answering the plan; this example shows Scout issuing it.

Prerequisite reading: [`04: generate-execution-contract`](../generate-execution-contract/README.md), the [World Model repo](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/world-model).

---

## The idea

> Scout owns intent → context plan. The World Model owns plan → context. The agent reasons; it never navigates the graph itself.

A vague prompt and a strategic one should pull different amounts of world. Scout decides the breadth from the intent; the world honors it.

## Walkthrough: `index.ts`

```ts
import { Scout } from "@meterless/scout";
import { WorldModel } from "@meterless/world-model";

const scout = new Scout({ intentRegistry: "./intents.json", policyPack: "default" });
const world = new WorldModel({ storage: "local", namespace: "scout-demo" });

async function answer(prompt: string) {
  // 1. Scout produces a context plan sized to the intent (NOT a fixed default).
  const plan = await scout.planContext({
    prompt, user: { id: "u-1", role: "ae" }, surface: "chat",
  });
  console.log(plan.contextPlan);
  // { subjectId: "account:salesforce:0015g00000ACME",
  //   sources: ["world"], maxTokens: 6000, relations: ["employs","has-deal"] }

  // 2. The plan becomes a read-surface query. The agent wrote none of this.
  const wide = plan.contextPlan.maxTokens > 16_000;
  const context = await world.buildPromptContext({
    subjectId: plan.contextPlan.subjectId,
    limit: wide ? 50 : 20,
    include: plan.contextPlan.relations,
    window: { start: Date.now() - 7 * 86_400_000, end: Date.now() },
  });

  // 3. Scout decides WITH the assembled, provenanced context.
  const decision = await scout.decide({
    prompt, user: { id: "u-1", role: "ae" }, surface: "chat",
    context: context.text,
  });
  return { intent: decision.intent.primary, entities: context.provenance.length };
}

const quick = await answer("what's Acme's primary contact?");
const deep  = await answer("build a full account plan for Acme next quarter");
console.log(quick.entities, "vs", deep.entities);
```

## Run it

```bash
# No @meterless package is published. @meterless/scout names your own
# spec-conforming implementation. With it on your import path:
npx tsx ./index.ts
```

## Expected output

```text
{ subjectId: "account:salesforce:0015g00000ACME", sources: ["world"], maxTokens: 6000, relations: ["employs","has-deal"] }
6 vs 41
```

Same world, same subject. The quick lookup pulled a tight neighborhood (≤20 → 6 entities). The account-planning prompt produced a wide plan (≤50 → 41), so Scout asked the world for far more context, automatically, from the intent.

## What Scout puts on the contract

| Field | Set by | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `contextPlan.subjectId` | intent + entity binding | which world node to center the query on |
| `contextPlan.sources` | intent risk/class | `["world"]` vs `[]` (skip retrieval entirely) |
| `contextPlan.maxTokens` | intent breadth | the read surface's `limit` |
| `contextPlan.relations` | intent capability map | which edges to traverse |

The plan is part of the signed execution contract, so "why did the agent see these 41 entities?" traces back to a specific Scout decision instead of an ad-hoc query.

---

## Why it matters

- **The agent never navigates the world.** It writes no graph traversal and picks no budget. Scout plans; the read surface executes; the agent only reasons over the result.
- **Context scales with intent.** A trivial question does not drag 50 entities into the prompt; a strategic one is not starved at 20. Breadth is a Scout decision recorded on the contract.
- **Provenance survives the whole path.** The assembled context returns the rows that produced it, traceable back through Scout's plan to the World Model events in one auditable chain.

## Next

- The reciprocal view, the same integration from the World Model side, lives in the [World Model repo](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/world-model).
- [`query-hmem-before-action`](../query-hmem-before-action/README.md): the same pattern, grounding in memory instead of shared state.
- [`scout-to-swarm`](../scout-to-swarm/README.md) · [`route-to-markovian`](../route-to-markovian/README.md): Scout's other downstream handoffs.

result: # Stack Overview The Meterless Runtime sits in the middle of the stack. During the day it answers requests from your apps. At night, Nightshift uses the same machine to run queued jobs. ```text Your apps Cursor, Claude Code, Gaia, Relay, Swarms, Meterless City, Sitcomify, DataPlant ↓ Meterless provider OpenAI-compatible, 127.0.0.1:8088/v1, meterless/* routing modes ↓ Meterless Runtime + Nightshift ├─ Day (Depth posture) serve every connected app, one lane per request └─ Night (Swarm posture) race queued jobs, scribes read, clusters form, judges and checks settle the Outcome Contract ↓ Open engines Scout Intent · H-MEM · World Model · Markovian · Swarm ↓ Your hardware Apple Silicon Mac · NVIDIA DGX Spark · Windows PC ↓ Kept work + signed receipts + Methods and Skills, on your disk ``` ## Layer by layer | Layer | What it is | Status | |---|---|---| | Apps | Coding agents, the free Meterless apps, the experiments, anything that speaks the OpenAI API | [Free apps](../products/README.md) and [experiments](../experiments/README.md) shipping | | Provider | One OpenAI-compatible endpoint with routing modes instead of model names | Contract public: [add-meterless-provider.md](../agent-ready/add-meterless-provider.md) | | Runtime and Nightshift | Local AI production control plane: jobs, fleets, lanes, checks, Outcome Contract, makes, receipts, two postures | [Nightshift](../products/nightshift/README.md): web live, Windows out now, Mac preorder, free Mac M1+ edition, DGX on request | | Intent detection and routing | [Scout Intent](../../engines/scout-intent/) | Spec + eval harness | | Durable memory | [H-MEM](../../engines/hmem/) | Spec + runnable reference | | State modeling | [World Model](../../engines/world-model/) | Spec + runnable reference | | Reasoning compression | [Markovian](../../engines/markovian/) | Spec + runnable reference | | Multi-agent coordination | Swarm orchestration | Ships inside the apps. Spec drop next, see [roadmap](../../ROADMAP.md) | | Quality, cost and latency routing | Runtime | Ships inside Nightshift. Spec drop next, see [roadmap](../../ROADMAP.md) | ## How the engines compose - **H-MEM feeds Markovian.** Memory seeds chunk zero of a long run and mines the output back into memory. The [memory-compounding demo](../../examples/memory-compounding-research/) shows the warm run finishing in 8 chunks instead of 12. - **World Model feeds H-MEM.** Sourced facts replicate into memory and answer scoped queries planned upstream. - **Scout plans before anything acts.** Downstream engines act only on its signed execution contracts. - **Markovian is the `deliberate` job kind.** In Nightshift, one long chain of chunks carries a compressed summary forward and checkpoints. - **All three together make a small model feel large.** Meterless City runs an 8B model with Markovian state, H-MEM memory and a World Model event log per character. Each engine's examples folder shows these pairings from its own side. ## Product surfaces | Surface | Role | Docs | |---|---|---| | Nightshift | The flagship: AI hotspot by day, overnight production by night | [docs/products/nightshift/](../products/nightshift/README.md) | | Gaia | Persistent workspace | [docs/products/gaia/](../products/gaia/README.md) | | Relay | Repeatable desktop workflows | [docs/products/relay/](../products/relay/README.md) | | Swarms | Coordinated, divergent generation | [docs/products/swarms/](../products/swarms/README.md) | | Experiments | What the runtime unlocks | [docs/experiments/](../experiments/README.md) | === markovian-with-hmem === # Markovian with H-MEM > Run it: `npx tsx index.ts` (uses the reference implementation in [`../../reference`](../../reference)). > **Marker note:** this walkthrough uses the XML alternate (``, ``) of the canonical bracket protocol (`[STATE_CHECKPOINT]` / `[TASK_COMPLETE]`). See [docs/marker-protocol.md](../../docs/marker-protocol.md) for the 1:1 mapping. [H-MEM](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem) feeds chunk zero with relevant prior memories, and the final run output is mined back into memory. Today's long run then informs next week's. > Memory enters at step 1 only. After that, bounded carryover maintains continuity. H-MEM is not re-queried every chunk. Prerequisite reading: [`docs/architecture.md`](../../docs/architecture.md), and the `01-add-memory` example in the [H-MEM engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem). --- ## The contract (from the how-to §13) ```text hmem.query ─▶ formatReinjection ─▶ memoryContext ─▶ Markovian chunk 0 ONLY │ ▼ run completes → hmem.ingest("plan_completion") ``` Heavy context enters once; the compressed carryover carries continuity forward. The completed run becomes a new memory for future runs. ## Walkthrough: `index.ts` ```ts import { Markovian } from "@meterless/markovian"; import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem"; const hmem = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "agent-cleo" }); const markovian = new Markovian({ chunkConfig: { chunkSize: 6000, carryoverTokens: 900 } }); const userPrompt = "Plan the Q3 analytics-warehouse migration."; // 1. Pull relevant memory BEFORE the run (past decisions, constraints, prefs). const { memories } = await hmem.query({ text: userPrompt, topN: 5 }); const memoryContext = formatReinjection(memories); // → "[infra] (long_term) Team standardized on AWS Glue catalog. {entities: Glue}\n..." // 2. Inject it into chunk ZERO only via memoryContext. const run = await markovian.run({ goal: userPrompt, memoryContext, // engine prepends this to step 1's prompt only stepFn: myStepFn, stopWhen: ({ output }) => output.includes(""), }); // 3. Mine the completed run back into H-MEM as a durable memory. await hmem.ingest({ eventType: "plan_completion", source: `markovian:${run.id}`, content: run.chunks.map((c) => c.content).join("\n\n"), }); console.log(run.output); ``` ## Run it ```bash # No npm package is published. This repo is an implementation spec. # Point the imports at your implementations of the engine contracts (see ../../AGENTS.md), then: npx tsx ./index.ts ``` ## Expected behavior ```text hmem.query → 5 memories (incl. "Team standardized on AWS Glue catalog") chunk 0 prompt includes that memory → the plan picks Glue WITHOUT re-deciding it chunks 1..N → bounded carryover only (memory NOT re-injected) run completes → hmem.ingest stores the plan as a plan_completion memory next week: a new migration run's hmem.query surfaces THIS plan as prior context ``` ## The closing loop | Phase | Engine | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | Before | H-MEM `query` | retrieves the Glue-catalog decision from a past run | | Chunk 0 | Markovian | the plan inherits that decision instead of re-litigating it | | Chunks 1..N | Markovian | carryover only; flat cost preserved | | After | H-MEM `ingest` | this plan becomes memory for the next planning run | --- ## Why it matters - **Memory enters at chunk zero only.** Re-injecting H-MEM every chunk would defeat the O(1) property, because the prompt would grow with retrieved memory each step. The contract (`memoryContext` → step 1 only) keeps Markovian flat and memory-aware. - **The two engines have complementary jobs.** H-MEM decides what past knowledge is relevant. Markovian decides how to reason through a long task without re-paying for it. Neither does the other's job. - **The loop makes long-horizon work cumulative.** A plan that ignores last quarter's decisions repeats them. `ingest("plan_completion")` lets the agent build on its earlier runs. ## Next - The `markovian-handoff` example in the [H-MEM engine](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem): the same loop, seen from inside H-MEM. - [`markovian-inside-swarm`](../markovian-inside-swarm/README.md): the other composition seam. - H-MEM's reinjection model: [H-MEM](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/hmem). === hmem markovian-handoff === # Markovian handoff > Cross-engine example: this folder has no runnable code yet. Treat the code below as a reference sketch of the contract. H-MEM is the memory a long [Markovian](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian) run starts from and writes back to. This example is the H-MEM side of the loop: what `query` serves into chunk zero, and what `ingest` absorbs when the run completes. > The reciprocal example, `markovian-with-hmem`, lives in the [Markovian engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian). It focuses on the chunked run; this one focuses on the memory contract feeding and closing it. Prerequisite reading: [`04-retrieve-and-reinject`](../04-retrieve-and-reinject/README.md), [`docs/reinjection.md`](../../docs/reinjection.md). --- ## The loop, from memory's side ```text hmem.query ──serves──▶ memoryContext ──▶ Markovian chunk 0 (once, never re-queried) │ ▼ run completes hmem.ingest("plan_completion") ◀──absorbs── joined chunk content ``` H-MEM does two things and nothing else here: retrieve the relevant prior decisions before the run, and mine the finished run back as a durable memory. ## Walkthrough (illustrative reference API) The code below is a reference sketch of the contract, not a runnable package. This repo is the implementation spec, and no `@meterless/*` npm packages are published. The `@meterless/hmem` and `@meterless/markovian` imports stand for your own implementations. ```ts import { HMEM } from "@meterless/hmem"; import { Markovian } from "@meterless/markovian"; const hmem = new HMEM({ storage: "local", namespace: "agent-cleo" }); const prompt = "Plan the Q3 analytics-warehouse migration."; // 1. Memory's job #1: retrieve what past runs already decided. const { memories } = await hmem.query({ text: prompt, topN: 5 }); // → [ "[infra] (long_term) Team standardized on AWS Glue catalog. {entities: Glue}", ... ] const markovian = new Markovian({ chunkConfig: { chunkSize: 6000, carryoverTokens: 900 } }); const run = await markovian.run({ goal: prompt, memoryContext: formatReinjection(memories), // enters chunk 0 ONLY skipSemanticMemoryAugmentation: true, // lower layers must NOT retrieve a second time stepFn: myStepFn, stopWhen: ({ output }) => output.includes("[TASK_COMPLETE]"), }); // 2. Memory's job #2: absorb the completed run as a new durable memory. await hmem.ingest({ eventType: "plan_completion", source: `markovian:${run.id}`, content: run.chunks.map((c) => c.content).join("\n\n"), }); // Prove the loop closed: the new memory is now retrievable. const next = await hmem.query({ text: "warehouse migration plan", topN: 1 }); console.log(next.memories[0].source); // → "markovian:" ``` ## Expected behavior (illustrative) ```text hmem.query → 5 memories (incl. the Glue-catalog decision from a prior run) markovian → plan inherits Glue WITHOUT re-deciding it (memory in chunk 0) hmem.ingest → run stored as a plan_completion memory, source=markovian: hmem.query → next migration question now surfaces THIS plan as prior context ``` ## What `ingest("plan_completion")` actually does | Step | H-MEM behavior | | --- | --- | | receive run content | classified as a `plan_completion` event | | mine | extract durable facts/decisions, not the raw transcript | | enrich | domain, entities, `source: markovian:` provenance | | store | written to the working tier, audited in the trust ledger | | later | eligible for retrieval, dreaming, and sleep like any memory | The completed Markovian run does not get dumped verbatim. It is mined the same way a chat or document is (see [`02-mine-from-chat`](../02-mine-from-chat/README.md)). --- ## Why it matters - **H-MEM makes long runs cumulative.** Markovian gives flat per-step cost; H-MEM is what stops the next run from re-deciding what this one already settled. Without the `ingest` step, every migration plan starts from zero. - **Retrieval feeds chunk zero, not every chunk.** H-MEM serves context once. Re-injecting per chunk would defeat Markovian's O(1) property. The memory contract respects the engine boundary on purpose. That is also why `skipSemanticMemoryAugmentation: true` is passed down: a chunked generator whose lower layer also auto-augments prompts with memory would retrieve twice. - **The handoff is provenanced both ways.** What entered the run is a `query` trace; what left it is a `plan_completion` memory tagged `markovian:`. The full round trip is auditable from the ledger. ## Next - `markovian-with-hmem` in the [Markovian engine folder](https://github.com/meterless/meterless/tree/main/engines/markovian): the reciprocal view, the same loop from inside Markovian. - [`world-model-sync`](../world-model-sync/README.md): the other "memory absorbs an external engine" pattern. - [`02-mine-from-chat`](../02-mine-from-chat/README.md: how `ingest` mines durable memory from raw content.

10: # Agent Planning Rule: Core Principles and Best Practices
11: 
12: This document outlines the mandatory planning protocol for all AI agents. The primary directive is to ensure all
13: actions are preceded by a transparent, user-approved plan. This rule is foundational to establishing a clear,
14: trustworthy, and effective interaction model.
15: 
16: ---
17: 
18: ## 1. Goal Description & Versioning
19: 
20: All implementation plans MUST follow a strict naming and header convention to ensure traceability and version control.
21: 
22: - **H1 Header Versioning**: Every implementation plan MUST use the format `# [Goal Description] (vN)`
23:   as its primary H1 title (e.g., `# [Setup Authentication] (v1)`).
24: - **Rule Compliance Reference**: A dedicated section titled `## Rule Compliance Reference` MUST immediately follow the
25:   H1 header. It must contain a bulleted list of the specific industrial rules (with relative links) being followed in
26:   the current plan.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## 2. The Core Planning Directive
31: 
32: All agents must present a clear, step-by-step plan before any implementation. The plan must be explicit,
33: actionable, and tailored to the user’s request. **Only after the plan is approved or clarified should
34: implementation begin.**
35: 
36: This directive is not merely a formality; it is a critical safeguard. By externalizing the planning process, the
37: agent minimizes the risk of misunderstanding, prevents "hallucination," and ensures complete alignment with the
38: user's intent from the outset.
39: 
40: ### 1.1 Primary Goal Persistence Mandate
41: 
42: The agent **MUST** carry over the original 'Starting Point' enquiry (the core objective) into every version of the
43: implementation plan. This goal must remain the primary heading of the document. Any shift in focus or addition of
44: sub-tasks MUST be explicitly documented as secondary or supporting actions to this primary goal, not as a replacement
45: for it.
46: 
47: ### 1.2 Architectural Boundary Verification
48: 
49: Before adding any execution step, the agent MUST verify it is not designated as 'CI/CD Managed' in project rules.
50: Local execution of automated pipeline tasks is PROHIBITED. If a script is for CI/CD, the agent must only modify its
51: templates or source metadata.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ---
56: 
57: ## 3. Components of an Effective Plan
58: 
59: An effective plan is built on four key pillars:
60: 
61: - **Clarity:** The plan must be written in plain, unambiguous language. Avoid technical jargon or internal thought
62: 
63:     process descriptions. Each step should be a simple statement of intent, easily understood by a non-technical
64:     user.
65: 
66: - **Step-by-Step Breakdown:** The plan must break down the request into a logical sequence of discrete, manageable
67: 
68:     steps. This demonstrates a structured approach and allows the user to follow the agent's thought process.
69: 
70: - **Actionability:** Every step in the plan must represent a concrete, executable action. For example, instead of
71: 
72:     "Gather information," an actionable step would be "Search the web for Q4 2024 financial reports from Google."
73: 
74: - **Tailored to the Request:** The plan should directly address the specifics of the user's query. It should not be
75: 
76:     a generic template but a custom-designed workflow that reflects the unique nuances of the task.
77: 
78: ---
79: 
80: ## 4. The Agent Planning Workflow
81: 
82: A well-structured interaction with an agent should follow this five-step workflow:
83: 
84: 1. **Deconstruct the Request:** The agent's first internal action is to analyze the user's prompt. It should
85: 
86:    identify the core task, the specific constraints, the desired output format, and any potential ambiguities or
87:    missing information.
88: 
89: 1. **Formulate the Plan:** Based on the deconstruction, the agent constructs a detailed plan. This plan should be
90: 
91:    a bulleted or numbered list that outlines the exact steps to be taken, including any necessary data retrieval,
92:    analysis, or content generation.
93: 
94: 1. **Present for Approval**: The agent presents the formulated plan to the user. This is a crucial checkpoint.
95:    The agent should explicitly ask for confirmation or for any necessary adjustments before proceeding.
96:    - **Browser Approval**: For manual testing plans, all browser-based tool requests are considered pre-approved
97:        unless explicitly denied by the user.
98: 
99: 1. **Execute the Plan:** Upon receiving user approval, the agent proceeds to implement the plan, step by step. Each
100: 
101:    action is performed as outlined, ensuring the process remains transparent and predictable.
102: 
103: 1. **Report Progress & Completion:** The agent should provide a final summary of the work done, confirming that all
104: 
105:    steps in the plan were executed. For long or complex tasks, providing interim progress updates may also be
106:    beneficial.
107: 
108: ---
109: 
110: ## 5. Handling Edge Cases and Best Practices
111: 
112: - **Ambiguous Requests:** If the user's request is unclear or incomplete, the agent must include a clarification
113: 
114:     step in its plan. The plan should state, "First, I will ask for clarification on `the ambiguous part` to ensure I
115:     proceed correctly."
116: 
117: - **Multi-Turn Conversations:** For continuous dialogues, a new, explicit plan is required for each distinct task or
118: 
119:     significant shift in the user's request. Simple, short follow-up questions do not require a new plan.
120: 
121: - **Exemptions to the Rule:** A plan is not required for trivial, single-step requests that have a straightforward,
122: 
123:     factual answer. For example, a request like "What is the capital of France?" should be answered directly without
124:     a planning step. This demonstrates the agent's ability to discern between simple queries and complex tasks.
125: 
126: ---
127: 
128: ## 6. Iterative Planning and Plan Versioning
129: 
130: The initial plan is a blueprint, not an unbreakable contract. For complex,
131: 
132: - **Categorical Alignment**: Group changes by their architectural layer (e.g., UI, Logic, Docs) unless they are
133: 
134:     functionally coupled.
135: 
136: - **Git Hygiene & Rebase Integration**: For tasks involving multiple branches or history refinement, the plan MUST
137: 
138:     include:
139: 
140: - **Hierarchical Mermaid Mapping**: Visualizing branch dependencies (referencing [Git Rebase Standardization
141: 
142:     Rules](./git-rebase-standardization-rules.md)).
143: 
144: - **CAM Table**: Mapping specific actions per commit to ensure logic isolation.
145: 
146: - **Workflow-First Priority**: If changes involve CI/CD workflows (GitHub Actions, scripts), the agent **MUST** fix,
147: 
148:     test, and verify the workflow functionality *before* arranging or executing commits. Functional stability of the
149:     CI pipeline takes precedence over documentation or stylistic refinements.
150: 
151: ### 1.1 Long-Running & Dynamic Tasks
152: 
153: For long-running or dynamic tasks, the agent may encounter new information or unforeseen obstacles that necessitate
154: a change in direction. In these cases, the agent MUST NOT deviate from the original plan without explicit approval.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 7. Industrial Planning Mandates
159: 
160: - **Environment State Check**: Every plan involving runtime verification MUST include a prerequisite step to
161:     confirm the application is running and accessible (e.g., "Verify App is live at `http://localhost:3000`").
162: - **Maximum Literal Detail**: Plans must be exhaustive and literal.
163: 
164: ### 5.1 Impact Scan Enhancement (Maximum Literal Detail)
165: 
166: For every DELETION, RENAMING, or REFUNDAMENTAL change, the plan MUST include a dedicated 'Surface Area Scan' to identify
167: and remediate all global references, internal links, and cross-file dependencies.
168: 
169: ### 5.2 Anti-Summarization & No-Truncation Guardrail
170: 
171: Agents MUST NOT summarize or collapse previously established literal details (file lists, exact commands, logic
172: branches) unless they are functionally obsolete or a mistake. Maximum clarity and non-ambiguity take precedence over
173: brevity. **The 'Change History' table MUST NOT be truncated.** It must remain a complete and literal record of all plan
174: versions (v1, v2, v3, ... vN) without omission.
175: 
176: - **Files:** Explicitly list every file (absolute paths) to be created, modified, or deleted.
177: - **Exact Commands:** CLI commands must be written exactly as they will be executed, including full arguments and piped
178:     operations.
179: - **Literal Payloads:** For operations like `git commit --amend -m "..."`, the plan must include the **literal message
180:     string** within the execution step, not just a reference to it.
181: - **Verifications:** Explicitly state the exact command or visual check used to verify each step.
182: - **Guardrails**: Restate the literal logic for handling conflicts, empty commits, and safety checks in every iteration.
183: - **Pre-Plan Context Gathering**: Information gathering (reading files, `git diff`,`ls`) must happen **BEFORE**
184:     the plan is finalized. A plan based on assumptions is a failed plan.
185: 
186: ---
187: 
188: ## 8. Temporal Hygiene & Change History
189: 
190: To ensure absolute traceability and industrial reliability, all planning and verification artifacts MUST
191: incorporate temporal data.
192: 
193: - **Execution Timestamps**: Every item in `task.md` and `walkthrough.md` MUST include a completion or event
194:     timestamp in the format `[YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm]`.
195: - **Change History Table**: Every versioned implementation plan (v2+) MUST include a "Change History" table
196:     immediately following the goal statement. This table MUST track:
197: 
198:     | Timestamp | Summary of Changes | Rationale |
199:     | :--- | :--- | :--- |
200:     | `[YYYY-DD-MM HH:mm]` | Concise description of the delta. | Why the change was necessary. |
201: 
202: ---
203: 
204: ## 9. Plan Versioning & SSOT Integrity (History Mandate)
205: 
206: **Iterative Planning** is the process of updating a plan based on new findings or changes in a task's requirements.
207: This practice ensures flexibility while maintaining the core principles of transparency and user alignment.
208: 
209: - **Plan Versioning**: All plans must be explicitly versioned (e.g., `implementation_plan_v1.md`, `implementation_plan_v2.md`).
210: - **History Mandate**: New versions MUST NOT overwrite old versions. Each new version MUST include the Change History table documenting all previous revisions.
211: - **SSOT (Single Source of Truth)**: Each version MUST be self-contained, restating all valid context and guardrails. Do not refer to previous versions for "missing details."
212: - **Fresh Start Protocol**: When a "Fresh Start" version (vN) is declared, all subsequent plans (vN+1, vN+2, etc.) MUST reset the 'Change History' and 'User Questions & Answers' to only include items from the declared fresh start version onwards. This is a strict exception to the full history mandate.
213: 
214: ### 7.1 Continuity Audit Mandate (CAM)
215: 
216: Before presenting a new plan version, the agent **MUST** perform a literal line-by-line comparison against the previous
217: version. Any dropped task, alert, or requirement MUST be either restored or explicitly listed in the 'Change History'
218: with a rationale for its removal. **Summarizing integrated logic from sub-plans is a violation.**
219: 
220: **Verbatim-Superset Construction:** When creating version n of ANY versioned artifact (plan, preview, walkthrough,
221: audit-log, summary, skill doc, release notes), the new version MUST be version n-1's text kept verbatim, with version
222: n's deltas appended — never rewritten, reworded, reordered, or selectively dropped (even with a Change History
223: rationale). Rationale entries in the Change History explain deltas; they do not license removal of previous content.
224: The deterministic construction is operationalized by the
225: `versioned-artifact-superset-build` base skill
226: (`scripts/build-version-superset.py`); the `planning-version-coverage-audit`
227: audit verifies the result post-hoc.
228: 
229: ### 7.2 Sub-Plan Versioning & Integration Mandate
230: 
231: All planning artifacts, including secondary or 'sub-plans,' MUST follow the versioning mandate (v1, v2, etc.). They
232: MUST NOT be edited in place. Once a sub-plan is confirmed by the user, its content MUST be integrated into the next
233: version of the main implementation plan while maintaining its full literal detail. **All subsequent updates MUST occur
234: within the main plan.** **Integration MUST be via literal copy-paste of all confirmed mandates.** Any modification for
235: 'brevity' is prohibited. Once integrated, the sub-plan is retired and redundant versioning is forbidden.
236: 
237: - **Propose a Plan Revision:** When a change is required, the agent must immediately pause execution
238:   and present a revised plan to the user.
239: - **Provide a Rationale:** The agent must clearly explain **why** the change is necessary.
240: - **Seek Approval:** The agent must explicitly ask for user approval for the revised plan before proceeding.
241:   This final check ensures the new direction aligns with the user's updated expectations.
242: 
243: ---
244: 
245: ## 10. Task Artifact Synchronization
246: 
247: Follow the status markers and include timestamps:
248: 
249: - **Initial Creation**: Create `task.md` at the start of planning with all top-level items.
250: - **Incremental Updates**: Update `task.md` after completing each significant milestone.
251: - **Status Markers**: Use `[ ]` for pending, `[/]` for in-progress, and `[x]` for completed items `[YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm]`.
252: - **Artifact Location**: All planning artifacts (task.md, implementation plans, walkthroughs) MUST be stored in
253:     the **main repository's** `docs/` directory (e.g., `docs/implementation-plans/<date>-<topic>.md`). When
254:     `ai-agent-rules/` is a Git submodule, artifacts MUST NOT be placed inside the submodule — doing so scatters
255:     planning history into a separate repo's commit graph. The main repo's `docs/` tree is the single source of
256:     truth for all planning artifacts.
257: - **Artifact Cleanup**: If everything is OK, we can remove the artifacts. The removal needs explicit user confirmation.
258: - **Compliance Mandate**: Every generated artifact (task, implementation plan, walkthrough) MUST strictly comply
259:     with **[Markdown Generation Skill](https://github.com/baneeishaque/ai-suite/blob/3786486bb54805fde12181bc8db34aaabede3e92/.agents/skills/markdown-generation/SKILL.md)** and
260:     **[Markdown Generation Rules Additions](./markdown-generation-rules-additions.md)**.
261:     This includes mandatory verification using `markdownlint-cli` before finalizing any artifact.
262: 
263: ---
264: 
265: ## 11. Status Traceability in Iterative Plans
266: 
267: To ensure absolute clarity during multi-phase execution, iterative plans (v2+) MUST track the status of proposed changes.
268: 
269: - **Marking Completed Steps**: If an implementation plan is updated during execution, any proposed change that has
270:   already been successfully implemented MUST be explicitly marked as `[DONE] [YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm]` or
271:   `[COMPLETED] [YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm]` within the 'Proposed Changes' section.
272: - **Visual Distinction**: Completed steps should ideally remain in the plan (to maintain context) but be clearly
273:   demarcated to differentiate them from pending work.
274: 
275: ---
276: 
277: ## 11. User Question Integration Mandate
278: 
279: To ensure maximum transparency and technical accuracy, the agent MUST explicitly address any technical or
280: process-related questions raised by the user during the planning phase.
281: 
282: - **Mandated Documentation**: All user questions and their corresponding agent answers MUST be documented in a
283:     dedicated **"User Questions & Answers"** section at the top of the revised implementation plan.
284: - **Traceability**: This ensures that critical clarifications and course corrections are captured in the
285:     Single Source of Truth (SSOT), making them available for future reference and audits.
286: - **Clarity**: Answers should be technically precise, referring to specific rules or protocols where applicable.
287: 
288: ---
289: 
290: ## 12. State-Dependent Phase Gating
291: 
292: Plans involving future states (e.g., Git history after 3 phases of changes)
293: **MUST NOT** predict or mock the result. They must instead define a **Protocol
294: Gate**: a set of mandatory discovery commands (e.g., `git status`, `git diff`)
295: and verification steps that the agent will run *at that time* to generate a
296: fresh, accurate preview for user approval.
297: 
298: ---
299: 
300: ## 13. Sequential Objective Protocol
301: 
302: To ensure absolute precision and user control, the agent MUST adhere to a strict sequential focus:
303: 
304: - **Single Objective Focus**: When instructed to perform a specific task (e.g., "update rules"), the agent MUST focus
305:   solely on that objective.
306: - **Deferment of Follow-ups**: The agent MUST NOT plan or prepare for follow-up actions (e.g., commit execution) in
307:   the same plan unless explicitly asked.
308: - **Verification Gates**: Follow-up instructions will be provided by the user *after* the current objective is
309:   confirmed complete.
310: - **Instructional Rationale**: When told to update rules, focus on updates ONLY. Do not jump to execution or
311:   downstream tasks until explicitly directed.
312: 
313: ## 14. Single Source of Truth & Content Integrity
314: 
315: The agent MUST strictly maintain the integrity of existing documentation:
316: 
317: - **Anti-Duplication**: Please don't duplicate things. We always need SSOT.
318: - **Audit Requirement**: When adding or updating something, the agent MUST read the file deeply and carefully. Only add what is missing.
319: - **Blending Strategy**: Blend new information into the existing documentation, or enhance the existing information. We always need single source.

### Add Meterless as a provider

Text modes in any app, with the real token and an honest offline state.

Add Meterless Runtime to this codebase as an OpenAI-compatible provider, next to the providers it already has.

The contract (Meterless Runtime 1.4, provider contract v4):
- Provider id meterless, name Meterless Runtime, default base URL http://127.0.0.1:8088/v1. Accept a pasted URL with or without a scheme, /v1, /v1/chat/completions, /v1/models or /healthz, and normalise it to <host>/v1. Never produce /v1/v1.
- Auth is real. Send Authorization: Bearer <token> on every call. The runtime writes the token to <stateDir>/proxy-token. Store it under the key meterless\_runtime\_token. The placeholder rt-local is rejected.
- Send meterless-app: <a stable lowercase id for this app> on every request, and meterless-scope: user on chat.
- Model ids are routing modes, not models: meterless/<disposition> (auto, fast, deep, cheap, local, fusion), meterless/<class> and meterless/<class>.<disposition>. Read them from GET /v1/models and keep any meterless/\* id you don't recognise.
- GET /healthz only proves the process is up. GET /v1/models decides: 401 or 403 is "unauthorized" (show a field to paste the token), 200 with meterless ids is "online", anything else is "offline".
- Auto Detect tries ports 8088, 8090, 8787 and 11434 on 127.0.0.1, localhost and \[::1\], and saves the first online or unauthorized hit.
- Plain text requests stay a string, exactly like OpenAI. Use a 180 s timeout, because a model load can take minutes.
- If the user pastes a connect link (http://<host>:<port>/connect#k=<key>), take the base URL from its origin + /v1 and the key from k. Never log it.

You are done when a wrong token shows unauthorized (not offline), Auto Detect finds the runtime, and a plain text request on meterless/auto returns a string.

# Meterless Engines Testing Guide

- **Applies to:** `angular-todo-app`
- **Last verified:** 2026-10-23
- **Test runner:** Angular CLI 22 unit-test builder + Vitest 5 + jsdom
- **Engine source:** browser-safe ports under `src/app/engines/`
- **Spec source:** a separate Meterless checkout; commands use `<meterless-spec>` as the placeholder

This guide explains how to verify every user-facing engine feature, what each test proves, how to run the automated suites, how to run the Meterless conformance and eval harnesses, and how to diagnose failures.

---

## 1. Scope

### In scope

- Natural-language assistant actions: add, complete, reopen, rename, delete, filter, list, and summarize tasks.
- Scout Intent routing, clarification, signed execution contracts, prompt-injection blocking, and destructive-action confirmation.
- H-MEM preference memory: remember, recall, forget, persistence, retrieval, and trust-ledger entries.
- World Model event log: task entities, upserts, tombstones, audit entries, and the Activity panel.
- Markovian plan generation: chunk configuration snapshot, marker cleanup, efficiency stats, and history persistence.
- Build, type, template, and CSS-budget verification.

### Out of scope

- Load testing, browser matrix testing, visual regression testing, accessibility certification, and penetration testing.
- Remote model providers. The current assistant is deterministic and local.
- Multi-user concurrency, backend sync, and IndexedDB migration.
- H-MEM dreaming, sleep consolidation, and conflict auto-resolution UI, which exist in the engine API but are not exposed in the app.
- World Model merge-review UI, which records proposals but has no operator screen.

---

## 2. Test layers

| Layer              | Command or entry point                         | What it proves                                                                | Runtime      |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| Unit               | `npm test -- --watch=false`                    | Store math, persistence, service behavior, engine-service integration         | jsdom        |
| Focused unit       | `npm test -- --watch=false --include=<spec>`   | One spec file in isolation                                                    | jsdom        |
| Named test         | `npm test -- --watch=false --filter="<regex>"` | One suite or test name                                                        | jsdom        |
| Component          | Included in the unit suite                     | App shell and engine panels render without template errors                    | jsdom        |
| Production build   | `npm run build`                                | AOT templates, TypeScript, bundling, and CSS budgets                          | Node         |
| Engine conformance | Meterless runner under `tsx`                   | Engine invariants independent of Angular                                      | Node + `tsx` |
| Scout eval         | Meterless eval harness under `tsx`             | Intent accuracy, injection recall/precision, tool routing, clarification rate | Node + `tsx` |
| Manual smoke       | `npm start` + browser                          | Real DOM, real `localStorage`, real clicks and keyboard input                 | Browser      |

---

## 3. Prerequisites

### 3.1 App dependencies

From the app root:

```bash
cd angular-todo-app
npm install
```

Verify the toolchain:

```bash
node --version
npm --version
npx ng version
```

Expected: Angular CLI 22.x, Node compatible with the app, and npm available. In this workspace `mise.toml` pins Node `26.10.0`; if your shell reports `mise ERROR No version is set for shim: npm` or `node`, run commands through the pinned toolchain:

```bash
mise x node@26.10.0 -- npm install
mise x node@26.10.0 -- npm test -- --watch=false
```

### 3.2 Meterless spec checkout

The conformance and eval runners live in a separate checkout:

```text
<meterless-spec>/
  engines/
    scout-intent/
      evals/runner/index.ts
      evals/fixtures/intents.json
      evals/config/thresholds.yaml
      evals/regression-set/v1/
    hmem/conformance/runner.ts
    world-model/conformance/runner.ts
    markovian/conformance/runner.ts
```

The app does not vendor the runners. Point the environment variables at the app implementations.

### 3.3 `tsx` for Node runners

The conformance and eval runners import TypeScript directly. Install `tsx` in the spec checkout or use a checkout that already has it:

```bash
cd <meterless-spec>/engines/scout-intent
npm install
```

If the runner reports `Cannot find module 'tsx'`, run from that folder so `npx` resolves the local binary, or install `tsx` globally.

### 3.4 Clean state

Tests clear `localStorage` in `beforeEach`. Manual testing should also start clean:

```js
localStorage.clear();
location.reload();
```

---

## 4. Ten-minute verification

Use this sequence when you only need a release-confidence smoke check.

1. Install dependencies: `npm install`.
2. Run the full unit suite: `CI=true npm test -- --watch=false`.
3. Run the production build: `npm run build`.
4. Start the app: `npm start`, then open `http://localhost:4200`.
5. In the assistant, run `Add a task: buy milk`.
6. Run `Complete buy milk`.
7. Run `Rename buy milk to get milk`.
8. Run `Delete get milk`, then click **Confirm**.
9. Run `Remember that I prefer short answers`.
10. Run `What do you remember about me?`.
11. Run `Plan my week`.
12. Confirm the Activity panel shows task events and the Memory panel shows one memory.
13. Reload the page and confirm the memory and activity survive.
14. Optionally run the four engine harnesses from section 12.

Expected: all assistant actions produce a success message, the task list and panels update immediately, and no console errors appear.

---

## 5. Command reference

### 5.1 Run every test

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false
```

Expected:

```text
Test Files  7 passed (7)
Tests       37 passed (37)
```

### 5.2 Run one spec file

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/assistant.service.spec.ts
```

Expected: 16 tests pass.

Other useful targets:

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/scout.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/memory.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/world-model.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/planning.service.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/services/task-store.spec.ts
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --include=src/app/app.spec.ts
```

### 5.3 Run one named test

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --filter="blocks prompt injection"
```

The `--filter` value is a regular expression matched against suite and test names.

### 5.4 List discovered tests

```bash
npx ng test --list-tests
```

### 5.5 Build

```bash
npm run build
```

Expected: `Application bundle generation complete` and no budget errors. The current initial bundle is about 232 kB raw, well below the 500 kB warning threshold.

### 5.6 Development server

```bash
npm start
```

Open `http://localhost:4200`. The app is client-rendered; the first paint happens after Angular boots.

### 5.7 Watch mode

```bash
npm test
```

Vitest stays open and reruns affected specs on change.

### 5.8 Coverage

Coverage is not configured in this app. The command below fails until a coverage provider is installed:

```bash
npm test -- --watch=false --coverage
```

To enable it, install one of:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @vitest/coverage-v8
# or
npm install --save-dev @vitest/coverage-istanbul
```

Then run:

```bash
CI=true npm test -- --watch=false --coverage --coverage-reporters=text-summary
```

---

## 6. Feature 1 — Natural-language assistant

### 6.1 What it does

The assistant accepts free text in the right-hand panel and turns it into a task action, a memory action, or a plan. It is local and deterministic; no network call is made.

The relevant files are:

| File                                      | Responsibility                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/app/components/assistant-panel/`     | Chat UI, input, pending confirmation buttons                            |
| `src/app/services/assistant.service.ts`   | Submit lifecycle, intent execution, task matching, user-facing messages |
| `src/app/services/scout.service.ts`       | Intent classification, risk assessment, contract signing                |
| `src/app/services/task-store.ts`          | The only task mutation point                                            |

## 7. Feature 2 — Scout Intent routing and safety

### 7.1 What it does

Scout classifies the request into a registered intent, extracts parameters, assesses risk, optionally asks a clarifying question, builds a tool plan, and issues a signed execution contract.

The app registry is `src/app/engines/scout/app-registry.ts`. The facade is `src/app/services/scout.service.ts`. Policy packs are `default` and `adversarial-tight`.

### 7.2 Risk and confirmation rules

| Risk level | Behavior                                                         |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `low`      | Execute immediately                                              |
| `medium`   | Execute immediately; no confirmation in the current assistant    |
| `high`     | Set `pending`, show confirmation, execute only after **Confirm** |
| `block`    | Show an error; do not execute; do not mutate state               |

`task.delete` is high risk. Requests containing `all` or `every` are escalated to high risk. The confirmation box exposes **Confirm** and **Cancel**; typing `confirm`, `yes`, `do it`, or `approve` also confirms; typing `cancel`, `no`, or `stop` cancels.

## 8. Feature 3 — H-MEM preference memory

### 8.1 What it does

H-MEM stores durable preferences and facts, retrieves them with a hybrid score, and records every lifecycle action in an append-only trust ledger. The app exposes remember, recall, and forget.

Relevant files:

- `src/app/services/memory.service.ts` — app facade and localStorage persistence.
- `src/app/engines/hmem/` — browser-safe engine port.
- `src/app/components/memory-panel/` — memory list and delete controls.

### 8.2 Data model

A memory record carries content, type, layer, timestamps, confidence, source, provenance, domain, namespace, entities, relationships, and optional supersession fields. A record without a source is rejected by construction.

The persistence envelope is:

```json
{
  "store": {
    "records": [],
    "seq": 0
  },
  "ledger": []
}
```

The ledger entry shape is:

```json
{
  "memoryId": "mem-1",
  "action": "create",
  "actor": "local-user",
  "timestamp": 1750000000000,
  "newState": {}
}
```

### 8.3 Retrieval behavior

The retrieval score combines semantic similarity, keyword overlap, tags, domain, entities, layer, recency, and a superseded penalty, then multiplies by confidence. The default threshold is `0.35` and the default top-N is `5`.

The app calls recall with threshold `0.2` and top-N `5`. If a generic recall query returns no strong match, the assistant falls back to recent memories so “What do you remember about me?” still returns stored preferences.

## User-Facing Improvements

| Improvement                | Mechanism                                | What the user notices                                                              |
| :------------------------- | :--------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Fewer clarification loops  | Context plan plus memory-aware Scout     | “The usual” resolves to the remembered preference instead of a follow-up question. |
| Grounded plans             | World Model context in chunk 0           | “Plan my week” names the user’s actual open tasks.                                 |
| Continuity across sessions | H-MEM recall and plan-completion memory  | A second planning run remembers the first plan’s decisions.                        |
| Bounded long work          | Contract-gated Markovian routing         | Long goals produce chunked plans with a visible stop condition.                    |
| Trust and auditability     | Pipeline trace and contract metadata     | The user can see which memory, tasks, and route were used.                         |
| Consistent facts           | One-way World Model to H-MEM sync        | Completed and archived tasks do not linger as stale facts.                         |
| Less repetitive typing     | Multi-intent execution and bulk previews | “Move all work tasks to Friday” becomes a preview plus one confirmation.           |
| Project continuity         | Optional project context                 | Project-specific tasks and preferences stay together.                              |
| Plan choice                | Optional plan alternatives               | The user compares a fast plan and a thorough plan.                                 |
| Research reuse             | Optional research intent                 | A repeated research question reuses prior findings and decisions.                  |

## Additional User Scenarios

| Scenario                   | Example prompt                                          | Engines used                         | Expected outcome                                                         | Phase |
| :------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---- |
| Weekly planning            | “Plan my week.”                                         | Scout, H-MEM, World Model, Markovian | A plan grounded in open tasks and remembered work preferences.           | 3     |
| Next-action coaching       | “What should I do next?”                                | Scout, World Model, H-MEM            | Three concrete next actions, each tied to a real task.                   | 2-3   |
| Vague reference resolution | “Do the usual for the report.”                          | Scout, H-MEM, World Model            | The remembered routine and the matching task are resolved before acting. | 1-2   |
| Bulk edit preview          | “Move all work tasks to Friday.”                        | Scout, World Model, TaskStore        | A preview of affected tasks, then one confirmation.                      | 5     |
| Completion review          | “What did I finish this week?”                          | H-MEM, World Model                   | A summary from durable world facts and recent events.                    | 4     |
| Project planning           | “Plan the launch.”                                      | Scout, World Model, H-MEM            | A plan scoped to the project’s tasks and preferences.                    | 8     |

| Explain why                | “Why did you choose that?”                              | Trace panel                          | The intent, contract, memory IDs, world entities, and route are visible. | 5     |

| Meeting follow-up          | Paste notes and say “Turn this into tasks.”             | H-MEM, Scout, TaskStore              | Proposed tasks and a follow-up plan, each requiring confirmation.        | 5-7   |

## Architecture
### Context-plan rules

The deterministic `ContextPlanService` uses these rules, in order:

1. `task.plan`: `sources: ['memory', 'world']`, `topN: 8`, `maxTokens: 8000`, `maxChunks: 4`.
2. `task.list` and `task.summary`: `sources: ['world']`, `topN: 0`, `maxTokens: 2000`, `maxChunks: 1`.
3. `task.complete`, `task.uncomplete`, `task.delete`, and `task.rename`: `sources: ['world']` for task resolution,
   `topN: 0`, `maxTokens: 1500`, `maxChunks: 1`.
4. `memory.recall`: `sources: ['memory']`, `topN: 8`, `maxTokens: 4000`, `maxChunks: 1`.
5. `memory.remember` and `memory.forget`: `sources: []`; the memory action itself owns recall.
6. `task.add` and `GENERAL`: `sources: []`.
7. Vague-reference markers (`usual`, `again`, `like before`, `my preference`, `remember`) add `memory`.
8. Deictic task references (`it`, `that`, `the report`, `this task`) add `world`.
9. Unknown intents fall back to `sources: []`; no speculative context is loaded.

### Contextual Scout scoring

The Scout port keeps its current deterministic score and adds one optional hook:

```ts
contextualScorer?: (
  prompt: string,
  intent: IntentDefinition,
  context: unknown,
) => number;
```

When the hook is present, the score is:

```text
score = clamp01(0.8 * baseScore + 0.2 * contextualScore)
```

This mirrors the existing semantic hook and preserves all existing behavior when no context is supplied. The app's
contextual scorer measures token overlap between the context block and the intent description, examples, and
triggers. It returns `0` when there is no overlap. The existing evaluation suite is rerun after this change; any
threshold regression blocks the phase.

### Contract gate

`PlanningService.planFromContract` refuses to run unless all checks pass:

```ts
const signatureValid = this.scout.verify(contract);
const expiresAt = Date.parse(contract.expiresAt);
const notExpired = Number.isFinite(expiresAt) && expiresAt > Date.now();
const intentAllowed =
  contract.intent.primary.id === 'task.plan' || contract.intent.primary.id === 'task.research';
const capabilityAllowed = contract.scope.capabilities.includes('markovian.chain');
const riskAllowed = contract.risk.level !== 'block';

if (!signatureValid || !notExpired || !intentAllowed || !capabilityAllowed || !riskAllowed) {
  throw new ContractRefusalError('The routing contract is invalid, expired, or out of scope.');
}
```

Refusals are shown to the user as a normal assistant message. There is no unverified fallback execution.

### Deterministic grounded plan

The app has no remote model. `PlanningService` therefore uses a deterministic step function that still exercises the
Markovian contract:

```ts
stepFn: ({ step, carryover, goal }) => ({
  content:
    step === 1
      ? buildGroundedPlan(goal, context.memory, context.world)
      : buildPlanContinuation(goal, carryover),
});
```

`buildGroundedPlan` includes the count of memories and active tasks, names up to three real tasks, and ends with:

```text
[STATE_CHECKPOINT]
COMPLETED: context gathered and plan skeleton drafted
REMAINING: sequence the work, identify the first three actions, and capture the next task
DECISIONS: grounded in the supplied memory and world context
CONTEXT: memory ids and world entity ids are recorded in the trace
```

`buildPlanContinuation` reads the carryover and ends with `[TASK_COMPLETE]`. The two-chunk shape proves chunk-0
memory injection, carryover, marker parsing, and completion mining without pretending to be an LLM.
